questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis C and cirrhosis presents to the clinic with complaints of fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and abdominal discomfort. On physical examination, you note mild ascites and hepatomegaly. The serum alpha-fetoprotein level is elevated. What is the investigation of choice in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic hepatitis C and cirrhosis presents to the clinic with complaints of fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and abdominal discomfort. On physical examination, you note mild ascites and hepatomegaly. The serum alpha-fetoprotein level is elevated. What is the investigation of choice in this patient?
questions.solution: rs for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) , such as chronic hepatitis C and cirrhosis, and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels, the investigation of choice is Triple phase CT. The preferred method for definitive diagnosis of HCC is a Triple Phase CT scan , which highlights arterial hypervascularization and venous washout. A triple-phase CT scan has the following phases: Arterial Phase - HCC shows hyperenhancement due to its arterial blood supply. Portal Venous Phase - HCC may appear isodense or hypodense as it becomes less conspicuous compared to the surrounding liver tissue. Delayed Phase - HCC exhibits washout, a characteristic feature - appearing hypodense relative to the liver parenchyma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
ng>:

The image given is that of Horrocks apparatus.

It is an apparatus used to estimate the chlorine demand of water (or the dose of

Bleaching powder that is required for disinfecting water).

Contents of the apparatus

  • 1 black cup
  • 6 white white cups (200 ml capacity each)
  • 2 metal spoons
  • 7 glass stirring rods
  • 1 special pipette
  • Starch-iodide solution
  • 2 droppers

Procedure:

  • A stock solution is made by mixing 2g (1 spoonful) of bleaching powder with water in the black cup and filling up to the brim.
  • The 6 white cups are to be filled with water to be disinfected up to about a cm below the brim.
  • With a special pipette provided, 1 drop of stock solution is added to the 1st cup, 2 drops to the 2nd, 3 drops to the 3rd cup, and so on.
  • Water is stirred in each cup using a SEPARATE glass rod.
  • After 30 minutes, 3 drops of the indicator are added to each white cup and stirred again.

Interpretation: The first cup that shows a blue colour will tell us how much bleaching powder is required. (n*2) where n = first cup which shows the blue colour change.
n× 2 is the amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water.

Hence 7 separate glass rods are necessary for performing this method correctly, not 1.

His laboratory tests are consistent with renal impairment. Which of the following features are seen in this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old male with a history of untreated pulmonary tuberculosis presents with symptoms of dysuria, hematuria, and flank pain, and noticed a gradual worsening of his symptoms. His laboratory tests are consistent with renal impairment. Which of the following features are seen in this condition?
questions.solution: ypically originates from the hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from the lungs or thoracic lymph nodes. The bacteria lodge in the kidneys, triggering an inflammatory response causing tissue destruction, caseous necrosis, dystrophic calcification granuloma formation, and scarring and strictures in the ureter. The putty kidney is a sequela of genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB) characterized by "extensive dystrophic calcification involving all or most of the kidney, seen as calcified non-functioning renal tissue. " It is the end stage of renal tuberculosis making the kidney non-functioning. Hematogenous spread and granuloma formation: GUTB typically originates from hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from the lungs or thoracic lymph nodes. The bacteria lodge in the kidneys, triggering an inflammatory response that leads to the formation of granulomas. Caseous necrosis and tissue destruction : If the infection progresses, it can lead to caseous necrosis, a form of cell death characterized by a cheese-like appearance. This process destroys renal tissue, impairing kidney function. Ureteric strictures and obstruction : GUTB can also cause scarring and strictures in the ureters. These strictures obstruct the flow of urine, leading to hydronephrosis (swelling of the kidney due to urine buildup) and further damage to the kidney. Dystrophic calcification : Dystrophic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts in damaged or necrotic tissue. In the context of GUTB, the extensive tissue destruction caused by infection, inflammation, and obstruction creates an environment conducive to calcium deposition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male is found dead in his apartment under suspicious circumstances. Upon initial external examination, petechial hemorrhages are noted around the eyes. The scene suggests a possible asphyxial death, as there are no overt signs of trauma. During the autopsy by the police surgeon, which among the following has to be opened first to identify definitive signs of asphyxia?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male is found dead in his apartment under suspicious circumstances. Upon initial external examination, petechial hemorrhages are noted around the eyes. The scene suggests a possible asphyxial death, as there are no overt signs of trauma. During the autopsy by the police surgeon, which among the following has to be opened first to identify definitive signs of asphyxia?
questions.solution: " data-dictid="ddba4206eb169277718335596e86da">cavity Explanation: In cases of suspected asphyxial death, the cranial cavity is typically opened first. The order of opening is the cranium, Thorax (Option A), abdomen, and neck. (To get a clear field of study for neck structures after draining of blood from neck vessels via the head and trunk) Asphyxial deaths frequently involve abnormalities in the lungs and airway, such as congestion, petechiae, froth in the airways, or other indicators of respiratory failure. This helps confirm if the cause of death is indeed related to impaired oxygen exchange or suffocation. Examining the heart may also reveal signs of right-sided heart failure due to hypoxia. Abdomen is first to be opened in stillbirth Order of Opening Cavities Head Injury Cases, Asphyxial Deaths The skull opened before the thorax and abdomen. Pneumothorax, Venous air embolism The Thorax opened first, then the skull. Abdominal cavity (Option B): While the abdominal cavity could be opened to assess for trauma or distension, these findings are less likely to provide direct clues in cases of asphyxia unless abdominal trauma is suspected, which is not indicated here. Stages of Acute Suppurative Otitis Media (ASOM)

Stages

Feature & Symptoms

Signs

Stage of Tubal Occlusion (Option A ruled out)

  • The Eustachian tube becomes blocked due to inflammation and increased blood flow, particularly at the nasopharyngeal end.
  • Mild hearing loss and earache. Usually, no fever is present.
  • Eardrum retraction, the handle of the malleus becomes horizontal, prominent lateral process of the malleus, and reduced light reflex.

Stage of Exudation (Presuppuration) (Option B ruled out)

  • If the Eustachian tube blockage continues, pyogenic bacteria invade the middle ear, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation.
  • Symptoms worsen, with significant earache that may disrupt sleep. Hearing loss and tinnitus may occur.
  • Redness initially on the pars tensa, followed by visible blood vessels along the malleus handle and the eardrum's periphery creating a "cartwheel" appearance.

Stage of Suppuration (Option C)

  • Pus forms in the middle ear causing the eardrum to bulge outward due to the pressure.
  • Excruciating earache, increased hearing loss, high fever (up to 102°F-103°F), vomiting, and possible convulsions.
  • A red, bulging eardrum with obscured landmarks, a hidden malleus handle, and a yellow spot indicating potential eardrum rupture.

Stage of Resolution (Option D ruled out)

  • The eardrum ruptures spontaneously, releasing pus and alleviating pressure.
  • Relief from earache and fever as the inflammatory process subsides. Symptoms improve with pus drainage.
  • Blood-tinged discharge initially, becoming mucopurulent.
  • A small perforation in the anteroinferior quadrant of the pars tensa is usually visible.
  • The eardrum's redness decreases and its landmarks become visible.

Stage of Complications

  • In severe cases, the infection may spread beyond the middle ear, leading to serious complications.
  • Potential complications include acute mastoiditis, subperiosteal abscess, facial paralysis, labyrinthitis, petrositis, extradural abscess, meningitis, brain abscess, and lateral sinus thrombophlebitis.

This is the primary reason for the decreased DLCO in patients with emphysema, as the reduced alveolar surface area limits the ability of gases, such as carbon monoxide, to diffuse across the alveolar-capillary membrane. DL CO (Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide) It measures carbon monoxide (CO) transfer from the alveolar gas to the pulmonary capillary blood. Carbon monoxide is used because it has a high affinity for hemoglobin, and its uptake is limited primarily by the rate of diffusion rather than by perfusion. Procedure Inhale gas mixture (CO and helium) Hold breath for ~10 seconds Exhale and measure CO concentration Factors Affecting DL CO Lung Volume: Lower volumes decrease DL CO (e.g., restrictive lung diseases) Hemoglobin Level: Anemia lowers DL CO ; polycythemia increases DL CO Carboxyhemoglobin Levels: Elevated in smokers, reducing DL CO Alveolar Surface Area: Reduced in emphysema, decreasing DL CO Pulmonary Blood Flow: Reduced flow (e.g., pulmonary hypertension) decreases DL CO Clinical Interpretation Reduced DL CO : Interstitial lung disease, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia Increased DL CO : Polycythemia, asthma, left-to-right cardiac shunts Significance in Clinical Practice Differentiate obstructive vs restrictive lung diseases Assess disease extent in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis Increased thickness of the alveolar-capillary membrane can decrease DLCO, it is more characteristic of interstitial lung diseases such as pulmonary fibrosis, where fibrosis thickens the membrane. (Option B) Decreased pulmonary blood flow can contribute to a reduced DLCO, it is not the main mechanism in emphysema. In emphysema, the primary issue is the loss of alveolar structures. (Option C) Hyperinflation of the lungs is a common feature of emphysema, it does not directly cause a decreased DLCO. questions.solutionHtml:
ion in the surface area available for gas exchange. This is the primary reason for the decreased DLCO in patients with emphysema, as the reduced alveolar surface area limits the ability of gases, such as carbon monoxide, to diffuse across the alveolar-capillary membrane.

 

DLCO (Diffusing Capacity of the Lungs for Carbon Monoxide)

  • It measures carbon monoxide (CO) transfer from the alveolar gas to the pulmonary capillary blood.
  • Carbon monoxide is used because it has a high affinity for hemoglobin, and its uptake is limited primarily by the rate of diffusion rather than by perfusion.

 

Procedure
  • Inhale gas mixture (CO and helium)
  • Hold breath for ~10 seconds
  • Exhale and measure CO concentration

Factors Affecting DLCO
  • Lung Volume: Lower volumes decrease DLCO (e.g., restrictive lung diseases)
  • Hemoglobin Level: Anemia lowers DLCO; polycythemia increases DLCO
  • Carboxyhemoglobin Levels: Elevated in smokers, reducing DLCO
  • Alveolar Surface Area: Reduced in emphysema, decreasing DLCO
  • Pulmonary Blood Flow: Reduced flow (e.g., pulmonary hypertension) decreases DLCO

Clinical Interpretation
  • Reduced DLCO: Interstitial lung disease, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia
  • Increased DLCO: Polycythemia, asthma, left-to-right cardiac shunts

Significance in Clinical Practice
  • Differentiate obstructive vs restrictive lung diseases
  • Assess disease extent in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis

 

Increased thickness of the alveolar-capillary membrane can decrease DLCO, it is more characteristic of interstitial lung diseases such as pulmonary fibrosis, where fibrosis thickens the membrane. (Option B)

 

Decreased pulmonary blood flow can contribute to a reduced DLCO, it is not the main mechanism in emphysema. In emphysema, the primary issue is the loss of alveolar structures. (Option C)

 

Hyperinflation of the lungs is a common feature of emphysema, it does not directly cause a decreased DLCO. Hyperinflation results from the loss of elastic recoil and air trapping, contributing to airflow obstruction but not directly to the decrease in diffusing capacity. (Option D)

questions.answerText: These drugs act by sensitizing skeletal muscles to insulin
questions.solution: sts/thiazolidinediones act on the PPAR (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor) gamma in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, sensitizing them to insulin and reducing blood glucose levels (primary action). Activated PPAR-gamma receptors enhance the expression of insulin-dependent glucose transporter GLUT-4 in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. Secondary actions: Suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis. Reduces fatty acid release. Promotes lipogenesis. Drugs: Pioglitazone (available in India). Metabolised by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4. Given only in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Side effects: Plasma volume expansion, oedema, weight gain, headache, myalgia, mild anaemia, and increased risk of fractures (especially in elderly women). C/I: Liver disease and CHF. Troglitazone (banned due to hepatotoxicity). Rosiglitazone (banned due to increased risk of MI/heart failure). Adiponectin (Option B) is released by the adipose tissue, enhancing insulin sensitivity. Gemfibrozil (Option C) impairs the metabolism of these drugs, leading to potential toxicity; hence dose of the latter should be reduced almost to half. Rifampicin does the opposite by inducing the metabolism of these drugs. Activating PPAR-gamma receptors in bones will lead to osteoclastic activation , resulting in bone resorption. Thus, these drugs can cause fractures, especially in those with osteoporosis (Option D) . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
sts/thiazolidinediones act on the PPAR (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor) gamma in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, sensitizing them to insulin and reducing blood glucose levels (primary action).

 

Activated PPAR-gamma receptors enhance the expression of insulin-dependent glucose transporter GLUT-4 in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle.

 

Secondary actions:

  • Suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis.
  • Reduces fatty acid release.
  • Promotes lipogenesis.

 

Drugs:

  • Pioglitazone (available in India).
    • Metabolised by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4.
    • Given only in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
    • Side effects: Plasma volume expansion, oedema, weight gain, headache, myalgia, mild anaemia, and increased risk of fractures (especially in elderly women).
    • C/I: Liver disease and CHF.
  • Troglitazone (banned due to hepatotoxicity).
  • Rosiglitazone (banned due to increased risk of MI/heart failure).


 

Adiponectin (Option B) is released by the adipose tissue, enhancing insulin sensitivity.

Gemfibrozil (Option C) impairs the metabolism of these drugs, leading to potential toxicity; hence dose of the latter should be reduced almost to half. Rifampicin does the opposite by inducing the metabolism of these drugs.

Activating PPAR-gamma receptors in bones will lead to osteoclastic activation, resulting in bone resorption. Thus, these drugs can cause fractures, especially in those with osteoporosis (Option D).

questions.solutionHtml:
order-top:1px solid #000000; vertical-align:middle">

DPT VACCINE

Protects Against

Diphtheria, Pertussis (Whole cell and Acellular), Tetanus

Dosage

  • 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks;
  • 1st Booster: 16-24 months;
  • 2nd Booster: 5-6 years

Route of Administration

Intramuscular, on the anterolateral aspect of the left thigh.

Adverse Effects

  • Local: Redness and pain at the injection site;
  • Systemic: Fever;
  • Severe: Persistent inconsolable cry (>3 hours), seizures, hypotonic hyporesponsive episodes, encephalopathy/altered sensorium, anaphylaxis.

C/I

  • Progressive neurological illness;
  • Anaphylaxis to a previous dose;
  • Encephalopathy within 7 days of the previous dose.

Precautions

  • Previous dose associated with fever >40.5°C within 48 hours;
  • Hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode <48 hours;
  • Persistent inconsolable crying for >3 hours, <48 hours;
  • Seizures <72 hours.

Storage

2-8°C; sensitive to light.

PENTAVALENT VACCINE

  • Protects a child from 5 life-threatening diseases – Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and H. influenzae type B.
  • Administer at 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks.
  • 0.5 mL given intramuscularly in the anterolateral mid-thigh.
  • Store and transport at +2 to +8°C.

 

Administer Pentavalent again to maintain immunity; severe side effects are rare (Option B):

  • The Pentavalent vaccine is only given in the primary series at 6, 10, and 14 weeks.

 

Administer DPT and monitor for severe side effects like encephalopathy (Option C):

  • While severe side effects like encephalopathy are possible, they are extremely rare.

 

No further vaccines are needed after completing the Pentavalent series. (Option D):

  • Even though the Pentavalent series has been completed, the DPT booster is still necessary at 16-24 weeks to maintain immunity against diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus.

questions.stemHtml: A 28 year old male presents to the STD clinic with a history of swelling in the inguinal region as shown in the image below. He has a history of unprotected sexual intercourse in the past few months and reports a painless ulcer, which healed without scarring. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Can be associated with hepatitis C co-infection

options.label: C
options.text: Presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy

options.label: D
options.text: Esthiomene is a complication in the tertiary stage of this disease

questions.answerText: Presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy
questions.solution: /p> Explanation: The given clinical presentation of a male with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse , swelling in the inguinal region (inguinal lymphadenopathy) and a painless ulcer that has healed without scarring is suggestive of lymphogranuloma venerum, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The incorrect statement is that it presents with an indurated ulcer and painless lymphadenopathy. Lymphogranuloma venerum (LGV): It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by serovars L1-L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis (M/C strain causing LGV: L2 ). It occurs in sexually active adults of all ages. It can cause LGV-associated proctitis in homosexuals, associated with HIV and hepatitis C co-infection. The incubation period of LGV is around 3-30 days , and the disease presents in three stages, described in the table below: Primary Secondary Tertiary 3-30 days Days-weeks Years after a chronic, untreated infection Small papule/pustule/ Non-indurated ulcer at the site of inoculation which heals spontaneously with no scarring. Lymphatic involvement of nodes that drain the primary lesion. Classic form: Tender unilateral or bilateral inguinal and/or femoral adenopathy (Groove sign of Greenblatt). The lymph nodes may coalesce to form a bubo or abscesses that may rupture spontaneously with the development of Fistulae or sinus tracts. There may be systemic features such as malaise and fever. Lymphatic obstruction due to chronic inflammation leads to fistula formation, strictures, and disfiguring conditions such as genital elephantiasis and esthiomene , which refers to hypertrophic enlargement with ulceration of the external genitalia. Diagnosis of LGV can be confirmed by the Nucelic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT). Antibody detection by real-time PCR can also be done. Treatment includes: First line: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 21 days. Second line: Erythromycin 500mg 4 times a day x 21 days. Third line: Azithromycin 1g weekly once x 21 days. Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3 (Option A): This statement is true; these specific serovars are the causative agents of LGV. Can be associated with hepatitis C co-infection (Option B): This statement is true; co-infections with other STIs, including HCV, are possible in individuals with LGV. Esthiomene is a complication in the tertiary stage of this disease (Option D): This statement is true; esthiomene (genital elephantiasis) is a recognized chronic complication of untreated or persistent LGV infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a history of profuse watery diarrhea and multiple episodes of vomiting for the past 3 days. On examination, he appears lethargic, has poor oral acceptance, and has dry mucous membranes. Laboratory tests reveal serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a history of profuse watery diarrhea and multiple episodes of vomiting for the past 3 days. On examination, he appears lethargic, has poor oral acceptance, and has dry mucous membranes. Laboratory tests reveal serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.solution: 9b1a73c6d">chloride at 0.5 mEq/kg/hour Explanation: Normal serum potassium level: 3.5-5.5 meq/L. Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L. Mild hypokalemia: 3 - 3.5 mEq/L Moderate hypokalemia: 2.5 - 3.0 mEq/L Severe hypokalemia: <2.5 mEq/L In this case, the patient has moderate hypokalemia with symptoms of lethargy and dehydration. Etiology: Common causes of hypokalemia in children include: Gastrointestinal losses (diarrhea, vomiting) Renal losses (diuretics, renal tubular disorders) Inadequate intake Transcellular shifts (e.g., insulin administration, beta-agonists) Clinical features: Muscle weakness Fatigue Constipation Cardiac arrhythmias (in severe cases) Polyuria and polydipsia Treatment: The treatment of hypokalemia depends on its severity and the presence of symptoms. In this case, with moderate hypokalemia and symptoms, intravenous replacement is appropriate. Potassium Supplementation: Indications for IV Potassium Supplementation: Symptomatic patients Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) Presence of ECG abnormalities Unable to tolerate oral feeds. IV Potassium Chloride Supplementation: Dosage: 0.5-1 mEq/kg per dose Administration: IV infusion over 1-2 hours Infusion Rate: Do not exceed 1 mEq/kg per hour Potassium Concentration: Maximum of 60 mEq/L for peripheral lines Maximum of 80 mEq/L for central lines Avoid using glucose-containing fluids to prevent insulin-mediated intracellular potassium shift. Oral Potassium Supplementation: Dosage: 2-4 mEq/kg per day, divided into 3-4 doses Common Preparations: Potassium chloride (10%; 20 mEq/15 mL) Potassium citrate (especially for renal tubular acidosis) Administration Tip: Liquid preparations can be bitter; dilute with juice or water to improve taste. Additional Management Considerations: Replace ongoing potassium losses Ensure volume resuscitation with normal saline Correct any associated hypomagnesemia Treat underlying conditions (e.g., monogenic hypertension, Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
9b1a73c6d">chloride at 0.5 mEq/kg/hour

Explanation:

  • Normal serum potassium level: 3.5-5.5 meq/L.
  • Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L.
    • Mild hypokalemia: 3 - 3.5 mEq/L
    • Moderate hypokalemia: 2.5 - 3.0 mEq/L
    • Severe hypokalemia: <2.5 mEq/L
  • In this case, the patient has moderate hypokalemia with symptoms of lethargy and dehydration.

 

Etiology:

  • Common causes of hypokalemia in children include:
    • Gastrointestinal losses (diarrhea, vomiting)
    • Renal losses (diuretics, renal tubular disorders)
    • Inadequate intake
    • Transcellular shifts (e.g., insulin administration, beta-agonists)

 

Clinical features:

  • Muscle weakness
  • Fatigue
  • Constipation
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (in severe cases)
  • Polyuria and polydipsia

 

Treatment:

  • The treatment of hypokalemia depends on its severity and the presence of symptoms.
  • In this case, with moderate hypokalemia and symptoms, intravenous replacement is appropriate.

 

Potassium Supplementation:

Indications for IV Potassium Supplementation:
  • Symptomatic patients
  • Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L)
  • Presence of ECG abnormalities
  • Unable to tolerate oral feeds.

IV Potassium Chloride Supplementation:
  • Dosage: 0.5-1 mEq/kg per dose
  • Administration: IV infusion over 1-2 hours
  • Infusion Rate: Do not exceed 1 mEq/kg per hour
  • Potassium Concentration:
    • Maximum of 60 mEq/L for peripheral lines
    • Maximum of 80 mEq/L for central lines
  • Avoid using glucose-containing fluids to prevent insulin-mediated intracellular potassium shift.

Oral Potassium Supplementation:
  • Dosage: 2-4 mEq/kg per day, divided into 3-4 doses
  • Common Preparations:
    • Potassium chloride (10%; 20 mEq/15 mL)
    • Potassium citrate (especially for renal tubular acidosis)
  • Administration Tip: Liquid preparations can be bitter; dilute with juice or water to improve taste.

 

Additional Management Considerations:

  • Replace ongoing potassium losses
  • Ensure volume resuscitation with normal saline
  • Correct any associated hypomagnesemia
  • Treat underlying conditions (e.g., monogenic hypertension, Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome)

"customMeta" data-dictid="b29a1a16ab1692777199ede1c6e28b">stain of corynebacterium diphtheriae showing metachromatic granules.

 

Albert Stain

  • Corynebacterium diphtheriae are slender bacilli arranged in V or L shapes (Chinese letter or cuneiform appearance), characterised by metachromatic granules (polar bodies, volutin, or Babes-Ernst granules) at the poles of the bacilli
  • Volutin granules are reserves of energy for C. diphtheriae, as polymetaphosphates are stored in them.
  • 4 stains can be used for staining volutin granules:
    • Ponder's stain
    • Loeffler's Methylene Blue
    • Albert stain
    • Neisser stain

 

Gram stain (Option B): It helps identify rod-shaped Corynebacterium diphtheriae, but does not help stain the metachromatic granules.

Zeil Neelsen stain (Option C): Only stains acid-fast bacilli ans is used in TB.

Gabbet stain (Option D): It is also known as Cold Zeil Neelsen stainand it only stains acid-fast bacilli.

questions.solution: and HPE findings suggest a diagnosis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis/Lymphocytic thyroiditis.. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. In histopathology, there is extensive lymphocytic infiltration with well-developed germinal centres. The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells (hallmark feature of Hashimoto's thyroiditis) . It is an autoimmune condition, so on hematological testing we see autoantibodies like Anti-TSH receptor antibody, antithyroglobulin antibody, and anti-TPO antibodies. Genetic cause of Hashimoto's thyroiditis is HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR5 polymorphisms. Long standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis can give rise to some cancers like: Papillary carcinoma thyroid Maltoma (a marginal zone lymphoma) {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

Cross fused Ectopic • A rare congenital malformation where both kidneys are located on one side of the body (unilaterally), with the ureter of the crossed kidney draining into the bladder on the opposite side (contralateral). • Presentations can range from incidental findings during imaging to renal impairment, depending on the function and anatomy of the affected kidneys. • Often identified through ultrasound, CT, or MRI, showing the kidneys positioned on the same side and their unique drainage patterns. Duplex collecting system • A common congenital renal tract abnormality is characterized by incomplete fusion of upper and lower pole moieties, leading to complete or incomplete duplication of the collecting system. • Duplex collecting systems may be associated with vesicoureteric reflux, obstruction, or ureterocele, despite being considered anatomical variants. • Imaging Characteristics : IVP can effectively image both collecting systems, but poorly functioning systems may not excrete contrast, resulting in a "drooping lily appearance" of the functioning lower pole moiety. {{caption_text}} Weigert Meyer Law • Ureteral Drainage : The upper and lower renal moieties each have separate ureters, each with its own orifice in the bladder. • Ectopic Insertion : The upper renal moiety ureter typically inserts ectopically, medial and inferior to the lower renal moiety ureter, often leading to a ureterocele. The diagnosis of a duplex collecting system is supported by the recurrent UTIs and imaging findings showing separate ureters, with the upper moiety's ureter likely inserting ectopically per Weigert-Meyer law, leading to potential complications like vesicoureteral reflux. 

The normal position of the lower renal moiety's ureter, as per Weigert-Meyer's law, is associated with a higher risk of vesicoureteral reflux.

 

Cross fused Ectopic

• A rare congenital malformation where both kidneys are located on one side of the body (unilaterally), with the ureter of the crossed kidney draining into the bladder on the opposite side (contralateral).

 

• Presentations can range from incidental findings during imaging to renal impairment, depending on the function and anatomy of the affected kidneys.

 

• Often identified through ultrasound, CT, or MRI, showing the kidneys positioned on the same side and their unique drainage patterns.

Duplex collecting system

• A common congenital renal tract abnormality is characterized by incomplete fusion of upper and lower pole moieties, leading to complete or incomplete duplication of the collecting system.

 

• Duplex collecting systems may be associated with vesicoureteric reflux, obstruction, or ureterocele, despite being considered anatomical variants.

 

• Imaging Characteristics: IVP can effectively image both collecting systems, but poorly functioning systems may not excrete contrast, resulting in a "drooping lily appearance" of the functioning lower pole moiety.

Weigert Meyer Law

• Ureteral Drainage: The upper and lower renal moieties each have separate ureters, each with its own orifice in the bladder. 

 

• Ectopic Insertion: The upper renal moiety ureter typically inserts ectopically, medial and inferior to the lower renal moiety ureter, often leading to a ureterocele. (Option D ruled out)

 

• Orthotopic Insertion: The lower renal moiety ureter inserts orthotopically, lateral and superior to the upper moiety's ureter, with a risk of vesicoureteral reflux. (Options A  & B ruled out)

questions.solution: The invertogram is crucial for assessing the most distal level of the bowel in male patients with imperforate anus, particularly when meconium is present on the perineum without an apparent perineal fistula. Proper positioning is essential for accurate evaluation. Invertogram Used to classify anal atresia in neonates by visualizing the distance between the gas bubble in the terminal colon and the perineal skin. Typically performed 24 hours after birth to allow for small fistulas to become apparent. The newborn is inverted from the lower limbs, with careful positioning to avoid hip and shoulder rotation. Remove any radiopaque items and ensure the X-ray is taken during full inspiration. Can cause discomfort and crying, which may lead to misleading results; a prone cross-table lateral view can be a more comfortable alternative. The invertogram is crucial for assessing the most distal level of the bowel in male patients with imperforate anus, particularly when meconium is present on the perineum without an apparent perineal fistula. Proper positioning is essential for accurate evaluation.

 

Invertogram

  • Used to classify anal atresia in neonates by visualizing the distance between the gas bubble in the terminal colon and the perineal skin.
  • Typically performed 24 hours after birth to allow for small fistulas to become apparent.
  • The newborn is inverted from the lower limbs, with careful positioning to avoid hip and shoulder rotation.
  • Remove any radiopaque items and ensure the X-ray is taken during full inspiration.
  • Can cause discomfort and crying, which may lead to misleading results; a prone cross-table lateral view can be a more comfortable alternative.

Invertogram image showing anal atresia

 

Plain abdominal X-ray (Option A): While useful for ruling out esophageal atresia and other anomalies, it does not provide specific information about the anatomy or level of the anorectal malformation.

 

Abdominal ultrasound (Option C): This is important for evaluating hydrocolpos and hydronephrosis in females with cloacal anomalies but does not assess the anorectal malformation itself.

 

Distal colostogram (Option D): This test can evaluate the distal bowel but is typically performed after a colostomy has been created, making it less relevant for initial assessment in a newborn with an imperforate anus.

eta" data-dictid="59ff8b38191692777201150e72ebc3">uterine filling and bilateral patent tubes.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG):

  • Visualising the uterine cavity & fallopian tubes by retrograde injection of radiocontrast dye to identify filling defects & blocks.
  • Timing of HSG: 
    • postmenstrual period
    • follicular phase 
    • usually D6-D11 of mesntrual cycle to avoid it during pregnancy and ensure endomtrium is thin for better visualisation

Preparation
  • NSAID 30 minutes before to prevent tubal spasm.
  • Paracervical block in patients with cervical stenosis.

4 phases of radiographic images taken
  • Pre-contrast preliminary.
  • During contrast filling.
  • Contrast spillage into the peritoneum.
  • During deflation and withdrawal.

Contraindications
  • Acute pelvic infections.
  • Active uterine bleeding.
  • Allergic to iodine.
  • Pregnancy.

Doxycycline can be given
  • If dilated tubes are identified (indicating previous pelvic infection).
  • As prophylaxis to prevent infections post-HSG.

Complications
  • Pelvic discomfort.
  • Uterine perforation.
  • Vasovagal reactions.
  • Dye allergy.
  • Intravascular dissemination of the dye.

Saline infusion sonography (Option A) or sonosalpingography uses ultrasound to visualise the uterus & tubes while simultaneously injecting saline (not radiocontrast dye) retrograde into the uterus.

Sonoelastography (Option C) is used to assess soft tissue stiffness.

Contrast-enhanced sonography (Option D) combines intravenous contrast injection & ultrasonographic examination.

questions.solution: n: Bochdalek hernia is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), accounting for about 90% of cases. The clinical presentation typically includes severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest, as seen in this patient . A chest X-ray often reveals bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, and immediate surgical repair is necessary. It is usually found on the left side (80%), but can also occur on the right (15%) or be bilateral (5%). Morgagni hernia(Option B) is an anterior, usually right-sided defect, often containing colon, and is usually asymptomatic rather than causing neonatal distress. Rolling hiatus hernia(Option C) occurs in adults when the stomach herniates beside the esophagus, causing reflux or chest pain, not bowel loops in the thorax. n:
  • Bochdalek hernia is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), accounting for about 90% of cases.
  • The clinical presentation typically includes severe respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest, as seen in this patient.
  • A chest X-ray often reveals bowel loops in the thoracic cavity, and immediate surgical repair is necessary. It is usually found on the left side (80%), but can also occur on the right (15%) or be bilateral (5%).

Morgagni hernia(Option B) is an anterior, usually right-sided defect, often containing colon, and is usually asymptomatic rather than causing neonatal distress.

Rolling hiatus hernia(Option C) occurs in adults when the stomach herniates beside the esophagus, causing reflux or chest pain, not bowel loops in the thorax.

Sliding hiatus hernia(Option D) is also an adult condition where the gastroesophageal junction and stomach slide into the chest, presenting with GERD, not neonatal respiratory distress

questions.answerText: Cost-benefit analysis compares monetary costs and benefits, whereas Cost-Effectiveness Analysis compares the costs to achieve a specific non-monetary outcome.
questions.solution: > Cost-Benefit Analysis It is a management technique that compares a program's monetary costs with its monetary benefits , expressed in terms of economic gain. It helps determine whether the benefits outweigh the costs in monetary terms. The main drawback with this technique is that the benefits in the health field cannot always be expressed in monetary terms . Cost-Effective Analysis Compares the costs of different interventions to achieve a specific health outcome that is not expressed in monetary terms. This process typically occurs within 18 to 24 hours after death. Gas production : H₂S Phosphorated hydrogen Ammonia CO2, Mercaptans and methane . Post-mortem blister Gas formation in the blood vessels can push blood stained fluid, air, or liquid fat between the epidermis and dermis, leading to the formation of small blisters. Post-mortem blister
  • Gas formation in the blood vessels can push blood stained fluid, air, or liquid fat between the epidermis and dermis, leading to the formation of small blisters.

Postmortem gas rigidity

Post mortem purge
  • Gas accumulation in the abdomen forces the diaphragm upwards compressing the lungs and heart, and the bloodstained froth exude from the mouth and nostrils.

questions.solutionHtml:
diagnosis in this clinical presentation is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion disease.

 

Prion Disease or Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathy (TSE):

  • Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles with no RNA/DNA.
  • Pathogenesis: Misfolding of normal prion protein (PrPc) to form beta-pleated configuration (PrPSc).
  • Histopathology: Spongiform vacuolisation inside the cell.
  • Associated diseases:

Types of prion disease
1. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (M/C)

  • Genetic: Familial form caused by PRNP mutation.
  • Transmission: Iatrogenic
  • Symptoms:
    • Dementia.
    • Associated pronounced involuntary jerking muscle contractions on sudden stimulation (startle myoclonus) and cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia).
  • Histopathogenesis:
    • Spongiform transformation of the cerebral cortex.
  • Prognosis: Uniformly fatal with average survival < 7 months after the onset of symptoms.

2. Kuru disease

  • PAS & Congo: red positive.
  • Kuru plaques: Extracellular aggregated abnormal PrP.

3. Fatal familial insomnia

4. Bovine spongiform encephalopathy

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?
questions.solution: p> The supraventricular crest is located within the right ventricle and separates the inflow tract , which carries blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, from the outflow tract, which directs blood into the pulmonary trunk. It is a thick, muscular “U” shaped structure extending from the interventricular septum to the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle. The crest provides the main attachment for the anterosuperior leaflet of the tricuspid valve. The septal limb of the crest is connected to the septal limbs of the septomarginal trabeculation (moderator band). Crista terminalis (Option A) Located in the right atrium - separates the smooth and rough parts of the atrium, not the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts. The moderator band (Option C) facilitates conduction in the right ventricle and contains the right bundle branch (RBB) . Helps prevent overdistension of the right ventricle during systole by acting as a stabilizing structure. It does not separate the inflow and outflow regions. Interventricular septum (Option D) separates the left and right ventricles but does not partition the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

The supraventricular crest is located within the right ventricle and separates the inflow tract, which carries blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, from the outflow tract, which directs blood into the pulmonary trunk.

  • It is a thick, muscular “U” shaped structure extending from the interventricular septum to the anterolateral wall of the right ventricle.
  • The crest provides the main attachment for the anterosuperior leaflet of the tricuspid valve.
  • The septal limb of the crest is connected to the septal limbs of the septomarginal trabeculation (moderator band).

    

Crista terminalis (Option A)

  • Located in the right atrium - separates the smooth and rough parts of the atrium, not the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

 

The moderator band (Option C) facilitates conduction in the right ventricle and contains the right bundle branch (RBB).

  • Helps prevent overdistension of the right ventricle during systole by acting as a stabilizing structure. It does not separate the inflow and outflow regions.

 

Interventricular septum (Option D) separates the left and right ventricles but does not partition the right ventricle's inflow and outflow tracts.

Correct answer B) Glycerol phosphate shuttle

The glycerol phosphate shuttle, present in white muscle fibers and neurons, specifically transfers electrons from cytosolic NADH to mitochondrial FADH2

Electron Transport Chain (ETC):

  • Location: Inner mitochondrial membrane. The ADP-ATP translocase in the inner mitochondrial membrane exports ATP to the cytosol and imports ADP into the mitochondria.. Atractyloside inhibits this transport process.
  • Function:
    • It plays a crucial role in oxidative phosphorylation.
    • Oxidation, which involves the loss of electrons, is central to this process and drives ATP synthesis
  • Shuttles:
    • NADH Shuttles: Glycolysis, which occurs in the cytoplasm, generates 2 NADH molecules per glucose molecule.
    • NADH cannot directly cross the mitochondrial membrane; it requires shuttles for transport.
    • There are two main shuttle systems: the malate-aspartate shuttle (Image 1) and the glycerol phosphate shuttle (Image 2), which facilitate NADH transport across the mitochondrial membrane

 

 

 

Property

Malate Shuttle (Option A ruled out)

Glycerol Phosphate Shuttle

Electron Carrier

Transfers electrons to mitochondrial FADH2

Cytoplasmic & mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase

Citrate shuttle (Option C) transports acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis, not for transferring electrons from NADH to FADH2.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with progressive bowing of the legs and tenderness in the lower limbs. The child has a history of limited outdoor play and a diet low in dairy products. Which of the following limb deformities is most likely present in this child?
questions.stemHtml: A 2-year-old child presents with progressive bowing of the legs and tenderness in the lower limbs. The child has a history of limited outdoor play and a diet low in dairy products. Which of the following limb deformities is most likely present in this child?
questions.solution: The scenario describes a child with classic signs of Rickets associated with vitamin D deficiency. This condition results in leg deformities in children with inadequate sun exposure and dietary intake of vitamin D. Clinical manifestations of Vitamin D deficiency Rickets (Option A) Occurs in children. Inadequate bone mineralization due to poor calcium absorption. Bones become soft and weak, leading to deformities under pressure. Clinical signs : Muscle weakness Delayed walking Skeletal deformities - "pigeon chest" (pectus carinatum) and genu varus (bowed legs), Genu valgum, windswept deformity. Rickety rosary Osteomalacia (Option C ruled out) Occurs in adults. Demineralization of bone, making them weak and prone to fractures. Risk factors: limited sun exposure, women after multiple pregnancies. Renal osteodystrophy Long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism can result in renal osteodystrophy, increasing the risk of pathological fractures. Blount’s disease (Option B) (tibia vara) is an acquired genu varus deformity typically developing later in childhood, while nutritional rickets, caused by vitamin D deficiency from poor diet and limited sun exposure, is more likely in this young child. Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option D) is unlikely because it is a genetic disorder affecting collagen synthesis, leading to brittle bones and frequent fractures from birth, rather than the progressive bowing of the legs seen in nutritional rickets. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The scenario describes a child with classic signs of Rickets associated with vitamin D deficiency. This condition results in leg deformities in children with inadequate sun exposure and dietary intake of vitamin D.

Clinical manifestations of Vitamin D deficiency

Rickets (Option A)
  • Occurs in children.
  • Inadequate bone mineralization due to poor calcium absorption.
  • Bones become soft and weak, leading to deformities under pressure.
  • Clinical signs:
    • Muscle weakness
    • Delayed walking
    • Skeletal deformities - "pigeon chest" (pectus carinatum) and genu varus (bowed legs), Genu valgum, windswept deformity.
    • Rickety rosary

Osteomalacia (Option C ruled out)
  • Occurs in adults.
  • Demineralization of bone, making them weak and prone to fractures.
  • Risk factors: limited sun exposure, women after multiple pregnancies.

Renal osteodystrophy

Long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism can result in renal osteodystrophy, increasing the risk of pathological fractures.

 

Blount’s disease (Option B) (tibia vara) is an acquired genu varus deformity typically developing later in childhood, while nutritional rickets, caused by vitamin D deficiency from poor diet and limited sun exposure, is more likely in this young child.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option D) is unlikely because it is a genetic disorder affecting collagen synthesis, leading to brittle bones and frequent fractures from birth, rather than the progressive bowing of the legs seen in nutritional rickets.

questions.solution: gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight” ), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice. Management: Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment. Cataract surgeries: ICCE (not preferred now) ECCE SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery) Phacoemulsification (most preferred) Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred. Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity. Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract. gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight”), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice.
  • Management:
    • Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment.
    • Cataract surgeries:
      • ICCE (not preferred now)
      • ECCE
      • SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery)
      • Phacoemulsification (most preferred)
    • Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred.

 

  • Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity.
  • Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract.
  • Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism.

Type of Anorexia Nervosa

Characteristics

Binge-Eating/Purging type
  • Recurring purging behaviors (e.g., laxative, diuretic abuse, self-induced vomiting)
  • Episodes of binge eating

Restricting type
  • Primary behaviors include dieting, fasting, and/or excessive exercise

Anorexia with dietary restriction (Option A): While this option describes a subtype of anorexia, it specifically refers to individuals who do not engage in binge eating or purging behaviors.

Bulimia with purging (Option C): Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (like purging) but typically occurs in individuals with a normal or higher weight.

questions.solution: nbsp; Hemopexin is a primary protein that is responsible for binding and transporting free heme in the bloodstream. When RBC undergoes hemolysis, heme is released into the blood. questions.solution: ibes Throttling (manual strangulation) . Throttling results in death through mechanisms like asphyxia (obstruction of the airway) and vagal inhibition (pressure on the carotid sinus leading to a drop in heart rate and blood pressure). The requirement of applying pressure for a minimum of 2 minutes to cause death is consistent with the physiological effects of throttling. Throttling (Manual Strangulation): Definition : A method of strangulation where the assailant compresses the victim's neck with their hands. Mechanisms of Death : Asphyxia : Obstruction of the airway due to neck pressure. Cerebral Anoxia : Restricted blood flow to the brain due to pressure on blood vessels, leading to potential brain damage. Vagal Inhibition : Stimulation of the vagus nerve can cause a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure, potentially resulting in cardiac arrest. Fatality Requirement : Sustained pressure for at least 2 minutes is typically required for lethality. Postmortem Findings: Examination Type Findings External Examination (Option B ruled out) Bruises and Abrasions: On the front and sides of the neck. Signs of Asphyxia: Cyanosis, facial swelling, Tardieu's spots, bleeding from nose and ears. Injuries on Other Body Parts: Additional signs of violence (abrasions, bruises, scratches). Internal Examination (Option C ruled out) Haemorrhages: In subcutaneous tissues under bruises. Muscle Damage: Tears or lacerations in neck muscles. Hyoid Bone Fracture: Significant diagnostic indicator, typically from inward compression. Laryngeal and Tracheal Damage: Fractures of thyroid and potentially cricoid cartilages. Haemorrhages in Mouth/Throat: Bruising and lacerations on the tongue, haemorrhages in mucous membranes. Medico-legal Questions: Determining Manner of Death : Suicidal Throttling : Considered impossible; hands would relax upon unconsciousness. (Option D ruled out) Homicidal Throttling : Presumed unless proven otherwise; common in homicides, especially involving vulnerable victims. Accidental Throttling : Rare, may occur during playful or affectionate contact. @Neet_pg_bot

ibes Throttling (manual strangulation).
  • Throttling results in death through mechanisms like asphyxia (obstruction of the airway) and vagal inhibition (pressure on the carotid sinus leading to a drop in heart rate and blood pressure).
  • The requirement of applying pressure for a minimum of 2 minutes to cause death is consistent with the physiological effects of throttling.

 

Throttling (Manual Strangulation):

  • Definition: A method of strangulation where the assailant compresses the victim's neck with their hands.
  • Mechanisms of Death:
    • Asphyxia: Obstruction of the airway due to neck pressure.
    • Cerebral Anoxia: Restricted blood flow to the brain due to pressure on blood vessels, leading to potential brain damage.
    • Vagal Inhibition: Stimulation of the vagus nerve can cause a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure, potentially resulting in cardiac arrest.
  • Fatality Requirement: Sustained pressure for at least 2 minutes is typically required for lethality.

Postmortem Findings:

 

Examination Type

Findings

External Examination

(Option B ruled out)
  • Bruises and Abrasions: On the front and sides of the neck.
  • Signs of Asphyxia: Cyanosis, facial swelling, Tardieu's spots, bleeding from nose and ears.
  • Injuries on Other Body Parts: Additional signs of violence (abrasions, bruises, scratches).

Internal Examination (Option C ruled out)
  • Haemorrhages: In subcutaneous tissues under bruises.
  • Muscle Damage: Tears or lacerations in neck muscles.
  • Hyoid Bone Fracture: Significant diagnostic indicator, typically from inward compression.
  • Laryngeal and Tracheal Damage: Fractures of thyroid and potentially cricoid cartilages.
  • Haemorrhages in Mouth/Throat: Bruising and lacerations on the tongue, haemorrhages in mucous membranes.

 

Medico-legal Questions:

  • Determining Manner of Death:
    • Suicidal Throttling: Considered impossible; hands would relax upon unconsciousness. (Option D ruled out)
    • Homicidal Throttling: Presumed unless proven otherwise; common in homicides, especially involving vulnerable victims.
    • Accidental Throttling: Rare, may occur during playful or affectionate contact.

questions.solution: g>Explanation: Gordon syndrome affects DCT. It is caused by mutations that increase sodium-chloride reabsorption via the NCC (Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter) in the DCT. this leads to low alosterone levels and hence it is also called Pseudohypoaldosteronism type IIA. It leads to: Hypertension (due to volume expansion) Hyperkalemia (due to reduced potassium excretion) Metabolic acidosis Low renin and aldosterone levels It is the opposite phenotype of Gitelman syndrome , which also involves the DCT but causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Inheritance Autosomal dominant (mostly) Pathogenesis Mutations in the WNK1, WNK4, CUL3, or KLHL3 genes result in abnormalities in serine/threonine kinases that dysregulate the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal nephron (Option A). This leads to increased sodium and chloride reabsorption, causing extracellular volume expansion and subsequent hypertension. Clinical Presentation Non-specific symptoms like muscle weakness, fatigue, hypertension (not always) Laboratory Findings Hyperkalemia Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis Hypercalciuria Low or low-normal plasma renin activity Low serum aldosterone levels (relative to hyperkalemia) Normal kidney function/normal glomerular filtration Management Correction of electrolyte abnormalities Salt restriction Thiazide diuretics @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
g>Explanation:
  • Gordon syndrome affects DCT.  
  • It is caused by mutations that increase sodium-chloride reabsorption via the NCC (Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter) in the DCT. this leads to low alosterone levels and hence it is also called Pseudohypoaldosteronism type IIA.  
  • It leads to:

  1. Hypertension (due to volume expansion)

  2. Hyperkalemia (due to reduced potassium excretion)

  3. Metabolic acidosis

  4. Low renin and aldosterone levels

  • It is the opposite phenotype of Gitelman syndrome, which also involves the DCT but causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

 

Inheritance

Autosomal dominant (mostly)

Pathogenesis
  • Mutations in the WNK1, WNK4, CUL3, or KLHL3 genes result in abnormalities in serine/threonine kinases that dysregulate the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the distal nephron (Option A).
  • This leads to increased sodium and chloride reabsorption, causing extracellular volume expansion and subsequent hypertension.

Clinical Presentation

Non-specific symptoms like muscle weakness, fatigue, hypertension (not always)

Laboratory Findings
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
  • Hypercalciuria
  • Low or low-normal plasma renin activity
  • Low serum aldosterone levels (relative to hyperkalemia)
  • Normal kidney function/normal glomerular filtration

Management
  • Correction of electrolyte abnormalities
  • Salt restriction
  • Thiazide diuretics

questions.stemHtml: Schematic diagram of sarcomere is given below. Red coloured structure is myosin with heads. Based on the length-tension relationship of muscle fibres, between which sarcomere length does the sarcomere allow optimal muscle contraction?
questions.solution: ="customMeta" data-dictid="4621bd564d16927771984726dbd76c">sarcomere is at perfect length—about 2.2 micrometres—the actin and myosin overlap perfectly, allowing the muscle to contract optimally. The sarcomere maintains full tension as it shortens from 2.2 micrometres to 2 micrometres, i.e., from length B to C. Sarcomeres are units in the muscles composed of actin and myosin filaments. The amount of force or tension a muscle generates depends on the sarcomere's length. Length A: Actin and myosin do not overlap; thus, muscle cannot generate tension. It occurs when the muscle is very stretched out. Length B: Actin and myosin start to overlap, thus generating tension - maximum tension occurs when the overlap is just right - 2.2 micrometre Length C: Sarcomere maintains full tension as it shortens from 2.2 micrometre to 2 micrometres Length D: When the sarcomere length is shorter than 2 micrometres, the actin filaments overlap, thus reducing tension. At about 1.65 micrometres, the sarcomere (Z disks) ends bump into the ends of the myosin filaments. Further shortening crumples the myosin filaments, and tension drops to zero. Thus, Length A to B: Muscle cannot generate any tension (Option A ruled out) Length B to C: Muscle starts generating tension, and the maximum is at 2.2 micrometres (Option B) Length C to D: Muscle can maintain full tension, and it allows optimum muscle contraction (Option C ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
="customMeta" data-dictid="4621bd564d16927771984726dbd76c">sarcomere is at perfect length—about 2.2 micrometres—the actin and myosin overlap perfectly, allowing the muscle to contract optimally.

The sarcomere maintains full tension as it shortens from 2.2 micrometres to 2 micrometres, i.e., from length B to C.

  • Sarcomeres are units in the muscles composed of actin and myosin filaments.
  • The amount of force or tension a muscle generates depends on the sarcomere's length.

  • Length A: Actin and myosin do not overlap; thus, muscle cannot generate tension. It occurs when the muscle is very stretched out.
  • Length B: Actin and myosin start to overlap, thus generating tension - maximum tension occurs when the overlap is just right - 2.2 micrometre
  • Length C: Sarcomere maintains full tension as it shortens from 2.2 micrometre to 2 micrometres
  • Length D: When the sarcomere length is shorter than 2 micrometres, the actin filaments overlap, thus reducing tension.
  • At about 1.65 micrometres, the sarcomere (Z disks) ends bump into the ends of the myosin filaments.
  • Further shortening crumples the myosin filaments, and tension drops to zero.
  • Thus,
    • Length A to B: Muscle cannot generate any tension (Option A ruled out)
    • Length B to C: Muscle starts generating tension, and the maximum is at 2.2 micrometres (Option B)
    • Length C to D: Muscle can maintain full tension, and it allows optimum muscle contraction (Option C ruled out)

questions.solution: plasia Explanation: The above radiological image of the “ hair on end " appearance, along with the history of multiple blood transfusions, indicates the diagnosis of T halassemia . Complications: “Hair on end" appearance of skull, maxillary bone overgrowth, compression fractures Increased osteoclastic activity (Option A) leads to bone resorption rather than the formation of new bone. questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with severe renal artery stenosis is admitted for hypertension management. The physician decides to prescribe a medication to control the blood pressure but must avoid drugs that could adversely affect kidney function due to the existing renal impairment. Which drug is contraindicated in this patient due to the risk of worsening renal function?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient with severe renal artery stenosis is admitted for hypertension management. The physician decides to prescribe a medication to control the blood pressure but must avoid drugs that could adversely affect kidney function due to the existing renal impairment. Which drug is contraindicated in this patient due to the risk of worsening renal function?
questions.solution: a-dictid="a66cd3adaa1692777182e77cb23021">artery stenosis reduces blood flow to the affected kidney, decreasing renal perfusion pressure. This decrease is perceived as threatening blood pressure homeostasis, triggering a cascade of events within the renin-angiotensin system. Increased angiotensin II levels help maintain GFR by constricting the efferent arteriole, preserving glomerular pressure despite reduced renal blood flow. ACE Inhibitors block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II, disrupting the compensatory mechanism and potentially causing a significant drop in GFR. ACE inhibitors can lead to acute renal failure in renal artery stenosis by reducing protective efferent arteriole constriction and worsening GFR. Beta-blockers (Option A) reduce blood pressure by decreasing heart rate and cardiac output. They do not directly affect renal perfusion or glomerular filtration rate. Calcium channel blockers (Option C) reduce blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels, including the arterioles. They do not significantly impair renal perfusion and are generally safe in patients with renal artery stenosis. Diuretics (Option D) help reduce blood pressure by increasing urine production and reducing fluid volume. While they must be used cautiously to avoid dehydration, they do not directly impair renal perfusion or GFR like ACE inhibitors. @Neet_pg_bot

Increased angiotensin II levels help maintain GFR by constricting the efferent arteriole, preserving glomerular pressure despite reduced renal blood flow.

ACE Inhibitors block the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II, disrupting the compensatory mechanism and potentially causing a significant drop in GFR.

ACE inhibitors can lead to acute renal failure in renal artery stenosis by reducing protective efferent arteriole constriction and worsening GFR.

 

Beta-blockers (Option A) reduce blood pressure by decreasing heart rate and cardiac output. They do not directly affect renal perfusion or glomerular filtration rate.

 

Calcium channel blockers (Option C) reduce blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels, including the arterioles. They do not significantly impair renal perfusion and are generally safe in patients with renal artery stenosis.

 

Diuretics (Option D) help reduce blood pressure by increasing urine production and reducing fluid volume. While they must be used cautiously to avoid dehydration, they do not directly impair renal perfusion or GFR like ACE inhibitors.

questions.solution: ong> The Sexual Assault Forensic Examination is designed not only to collect evidence but also to ensure that victims receive necessary medical treatment, addressing both physical health and immediate care needs. Sexual Assault Forensic Examination Kit (also known as a rape kit) Purpose : Preserves DNA evidence from the body, clothes, or personal items after a sexual assault and provides important medical care. No Requirement to Report : Victims can undergo an exam without reporting the crime, allowing evidence to be stored in case of later reporting. (Option C ruled out) Contents : The kit includes items like swabs, bags, documentation forms, and instructions for evidence collection (contents may vary by location). Exam Procedure : Typically includes immediate medical care, health history review, head-to-toe examination, evidence collection (e.g., DNA, blood, hair samples), and documentation of injuries. Follow-Up Care : Includes treatment for STIs, emergency contraception, and resources for further medical support. Examiners : These are conducted by trained professionals like Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners (SANEs) or Sexual Assault Forensic Examiners (SAFEs). Benefits : Helps in potential prosecution, connects DNA to databases for future investigations, and addresses physical health needs after an assault. The examination focuses solely on collecting evidence and does not provide medical treatment (Option A) : This option is incorrect. While evidence collection is a key component, the Sexual Assault Forensic Examination also includes important medical care, such as treating injuries and providing preventive measures for STIs and emergency contraception. The examination is primarily for legal purposes and does not address the psychological well-being of the victim (Option D) : Sexual Assault Forensic Examination does take into account the psychological well-being of the victim, often providing access to mental health resources and support during and after the examination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: st Zenker’s diverticulum , an outpouching occurring at a site known as Killian’s Dehiscence (often referred to as the "gateway of tears"). This space is formed by the two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle: the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibres) and the cricopharyngeus (transverse fibres) . This arrangement creates a triangular gap known as Killian’s dehiscence . Zenker’s Diverticulum (Hypopharyngeal Pouch/Pharyngeal Pouch): Description An acquired, false, and pulsion diverticulum formed by the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian's dehiscence. Clinical manifestations Dysphagia Regurgitation Food getting stuck (leading to coughing while eating) Aspiration Halitosis (bad breath) Investigation Barium swallow reveals an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa above the upper oesophagal sphincter, often with slow emptying of the diverticulum. Management Diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeal myotomy: Surgical removal of the diverticulum and myotomy of the cricopharyngeal muscle. Diverticular suspension: Dissection and inversion of the diverticulum with its apex pointing cranially. Myotomy through stapler transection: Transoral insertion of a linear stapler to divide the septum between the diverticulum and the true oesophagal lumen. Dohlman Procedure: Endoscopic technique involving division of the diverticulum wall and cricopharyngeal myotomy. Cricopharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option A): Incorrect because Zenker’s diverticulum arises above the esophagus, not between these structures. Thyropharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option B): Incorrect, as the esophagus lies inferior to the area of dehiscence. Inferior constrictor along with upper esophageal muscle fibres (Option D): Incorrect because this does not specify the true anatomical gap (Killian’s dehiscence is between the two parts of the inferior constrictor, not between it and the esophagus). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
st Zenker’s diverticulum, an outpouching occurring at a site known as Killian’s Dehiscence (often referred to as the "gateway of tears").
  • This space is formed by the two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle: the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibres) and the cricopharyngeus (transverse fibres). This arrangement creates a triangular gap known as Killian’s dehiscence.

    •  

    Zenker’s Diverticulum (Hypopharyngeal Pouch/Pharyngeal Pouch):

    Description

    An acquired, false, and pulsion diverticulum formed by the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian's dehiscence.

    Clinical manifestations
    • Dysphagia
    • Regurgitation
    • Food getting stuck (leading to coughing while eating)
    • Aspiration
    • Halitosis (bad breath)

    Investigation

    Barium swallow reveals an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa above the upper oesophagal sphincter, often with slow emptying of the diverticulum.

     

    Management

    • Diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeal myotomy: Surgical removal of the diverticulum and myotomy of the cricopharyngeal muscle.
    • Diverticular suspension: Dissection and inversion of the diverticulum with its apex pointing cranially.
    • Myotomy through stapler transection: Transoral insertion of a linear stapler to divide the septum between the diverticulum and the true oesophagal lumen.

    Dohlman Procedure: Endoscopic technique involving division of the diverticulum wall and cricopharyngeal myotomy.

     

     

    Cricopharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option A): Incorrect because Zenker’s diverticulum arises above the esophagus, not between these structures.

    Thyropharyngeus and esophageal muscle fibres (Option B): Incorrect, as the esophagus lies inferior to the area of dehiscence.

    Inferior constrictor along with upper esophageal muscle fibres (Option D): Incorrect because this does not specify the true anatomical gap (Killian’s dehiscence is between the two parts of the inferior constrictor, not between it and the esophagus).

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with cyanotic spells and a chest x-ray as shown below. Which of the following investigations is considered the gold standard for diagnosing and characterizing this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-month-old infant presents with cyanotic spells and a chest x-ray as shown below. Which of the following investigations is considered the gold standard for diagnosing and characterizing this condition?
questions.solution: Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosing and characterizing Tetralogy of Fallot. It provides detailed information about the aortic override, RVOT obstruction, and the sizes of related structures such as the pulmonary valve annulus and the pulmonary arteries. I nvestigation of ToF Physical Examination: Cyanosis, clubbing, heart murmur, intensity/character of murmur, presence of thrill Chest X-ray: (Option B ruled out) Enlarged right ventricle, "boot-shaped" heart , decreased pulmonary vascular markings, right-sided aortic arch (20% of cases) Electrocardiogram (ECG): (Option A ruled out) Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH), dominant R wave in V1/V2, RSR' pattern, tall P waves indicating right atrial enlargement Echocardiography: (Gold standard) (Option D) Assessment of: Aortic override RVOT obstruction Size of pulmonary valve annulus, main pulmonary artery, proximal branch pulmonary arteries Presence of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) Cardiac Catheterization: (Option C ruled out) Indications: Conclusive anatomy information needed Suspicion of coronary artery anomalies ToF with pulmonary atresia Measure pressures and oxygen saturations Perform interventions (e.g., Blalock-Taussig shunt) Treatment of ToF: Management of Tet Spells Immediate interventions: Knee-chest position Oxygen administration Morphine for sedation Intravenous fluids Surgical Repair Complete Repair Procedure: Close VSD, relieve RVOT obstruction Approach: Transatrial-transpulmonary Considerations: Minimizing pulmonary insufficiency with smaller patches Palliative Shunts Blalock-Taussig Shunt : Connects subclavian artery to pulmonary artery Central Shunt : Connects ascending aorta to main pulmonary artery @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosing and characterizing Tetralogy of Fallot.
  • It provides detailed information about the aortic override, RVOT obstruction, and the sizes of related structures such as the pulmonary valve annulus and the pulmonary arteries.

    • Investigation of ToF

    • Physical Examination:
      • Cyanosis, clubbing, heart murmur, intensity/character of murmur, presence of thrill
    • Chest X-ray: (Option B ruled out)
      • Enlarged right ventricle, "boot-shaped" heart, decreased pulmonary vascular markings, right-sided aortic arch (20% of cases)
    • Electrocardiogram (ECG): (Option A ruled out)
      • Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH), dominant R wave in V1/V2, RSR' pattern, tall P waves indicating right atrial enlargement
    • Echocardiography: (Gold standard) (Option D)
      • Assessment of:
        • Aortic override
        • RVOT obstruction
        • Size of pulmonary valve annulus, main pulmonary artery, proximal branch pulmonary arteries
        • Presence of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
    • Cardiac Catheterization: (Option C ruled out)
      • Indications:
        • Conclusive anatomy information needed
        • Suspicion of coronary artery anomalies
        • ToF with pulmonary atresia
        • Measure pressures and oxygen saturations
        • Perform interventions (e.g., Blalock-Taussig shunt)

    Treatment of ToF:

    • Management of Tet Spells
      • Immediate interventions:
        • Knee-chest position
        • Oxygen administration
        • Morphine for sedation
        • Intravenous fluids
    • Surgical Repair
      • Complete Repair
        • Procedure: Close VSD, relieve RVOT obstruction
        • Approach: Transatrial-transpulmonary
        • Considerations: Minimizing pulmonary insufficiency with smaller patches
      • Palliative Shunts
        • Blalock-Taussig Shunt: Connects subclavian artery to pulmonary artery
        • Central Shunt: Connects ascending aorta to main pulmonary artery

questions.solution: tient from a rural area in Africa presents with fever, headache, and night sweats, along with the characteristic posterior cervical lymphadenopathy seen in the image. These findings are typical of African sleeping sickness . The disease is transmitted by the tsetse fly ( Glossina species) and exists in two forms: West African sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense , which classically presents with Winterbottom’s sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy), and East African sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense . Leptospirosis (Option C): This can present with fever and systemic symptoms, but it usually does not cause significant cervical lymphadenopathy or distinctive sleep pattern changes. Malaria (Option B): While malaria presents with fever and malaise, it typically involves symptoms such as chills and rigours, and does not usually lead to the sleep disturbances seen in sleeping sickness. Dengue fever(Option D): This can cause fever and malaise but is less likely to produce the specific symptoms of sleep disturbances and lymphadenopathy described. @Neet_pg_bot
