questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue and muscle weakness. Laboratory tests reveal hypoglycemia and elevated lactate levels. The physician suspects a deficiency in a coenzyme essential for gluconeogenesis. Which coenzyme is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue and muscle weakness. Laboratory tests reveal hypoglycemia and elevated lactate levels. The physician suspects a deficiency in a coenzyme essential for gluconeogenesis. Which coenzyme is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct answer C) Biotin Biotin is a crucial coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase , which catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, the first regulatory step of gluconeogenesis. This reaction occurs in mitochondria and is essential for maintaining blood glucose levels during fasting. Biotin also functions as a coenzyme for propionyl-CoA carboxylase , which is involved in odd-chain fatty acid metabolism. Biotin deficiency leads to decreased gluconeogenesis , causing hypoglycemia and elevated lactate levels due to impaired conversion of pyruvate to glucose. Causes of biotin deficiency include: Severe malnutrition Consumption of raw eggs (contain avidin , which binds biotin and prevents its absorption) Inherited metabolic disorders (e.g., autosomal recessive biotinidase deficiency or holo-carboxylase synthetase deficiency ) Gluconeogenesis & Coenzymes Step Enzyme Required Coenzyme Location Pyruvate → Oxaloacetate Pyruvate carboxylase Biotin Mitochondria Oxaloacetate → PEP PEPCK GTP Cytoplasm/Mitochondria F-1,6-BP → F-6-P Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase Mg²⁺ Cytoplasm G-6-P → Glucose Glucose-6-phosphatase Mg²⁺ Endoplasmic Reticulum Magnesium (Option A): Required for ATP-dependent reactions but does not function as a coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase. Thiamine Pyrophosphate (Option B): Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase , not for gluconeogenesis. Fluoride (Option D): Inhibits enolase in glycolysis but has no role in gluconeogenesis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer C) Biotin

  • Biotin is a crucial coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, the first regulatory step of gluconeogenesis.
  • This reaction occurs in mitochondria and is essential for maintaining blood glucose levels during fasting.

  • Biotin also functions as a coenzyme for propionyl-CoA carboxylase, which is involved in odd-chain fatty acid metabolism.
  • Biotin deficiency leads to decreased gluconeogenesis, causing hypoglycemia and elevated lactate levels due to impaired conversion of pyruvate to glucose.
  • Causes of biotin deficiency include:
    • Severe malnutrition
    • Consumption of raw eggs (contain avidin, which binds biotin and prevents its absorption)
    • Inherited metabolic disorders (e.g., autosomal recessive biotinidase deficiency or holo-carboxylase synthetase deficiency)

Gluconeogenesis & Coenzymes

Step Enzyme Required Coenzyme Location
Pyruvate → Oxaloacetate Pyruvate carboxylase Biotin Mitochondria
Oxaloacetate → PEP PEPCK GTP Cytoplasm/Mitochondria
F-1,6-BP → F-6-P Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase Mg²⁺ Cytoplasm
G-6-P → Glucose Glucose-6-phosphatase Mg²⁺ Endoplasmic Reticulum

Magnesium (Option A): Required for ATP-dependent reactions but does not function as a coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase.

Thiamine Pyrophosphate (Option B): Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, not for gluconeogenesis.

Fluoride (Option D): Inhibits enolase in glycolysis but has no role in gluconeogenesis.

She also reports trouble with colour perception. Fundoscopic examination reveals the findings shown in the image. Which type of optic neuritis is most likely to be seen?
questions.solution: undoscopy suggests Neuroretinitis , a subtype of optic neuritis. Optic neuritis is an inflammatory condition of the optic nerve that can cause vision loss, with symptoms including decreased vision, pain in eye movement, and visual field defects. Classification of Optic neuritis: Papillitis (Option A) Retrobulbar Neuritis (Option B) Neuroretinitis (Option C) Site Optic disc Optic nerve behind the eyeball. Optic disc and surrounding retina in the macular area. Characteristic features Fundoscopy reveals a blurred disc margin due to leakage and increased capillary permeability, edematous and hyperaemic disc, and physiological cup is obliterated. Pain on eye elevation RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect) is observed. Fundoscopic examination typically reveals normal optic disc , at least initially, which is why the classic phrase, “ the patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing ” is often used to describe retrobulbar neuritis. A macular star is seen in fundoscopy (accumulation of lipids). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl presents with monthly cyclic abdominal pain for the past year. She has not yet experienced menarche. The patient appears well-developed for her age, with normal secondary sexual characteristics. External genital examination reveals the following. An ultrasound of the pelvis reveals a distended vagina filled with blood, but the uterus and ovaries appear normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl presents with monthly cyclic abdominal pain for the past year. She has not yet experienced menarche. The patient appears well-developed for her age, with normal secondary sexual characteristics. External genital examination reveals the following. An ultrasound of the pelvis reveals a distended vagina filled with blood, but the uterus and ovaries appear normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: resentation of cyclic abdominal pain, the absence of menarche, and the finding of a bulging, bluish hymen on physical examination are characteristics of an imperforate hymen causing cryptomenorrhea . This condition leads to the accumulation of menstrual blood behind the hymen, which explains the distended vagina observed on ultrasound. Cryptomenorrhea Definition Obstruction of menstrual blood outflow due to congenital malformations Common Causes Imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum, vaginal agenesis, cervical stenosis Symptoms/ Complications Primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, abdominal mass, acute urinary retention, endometriosis, iatrogenic infections Physical Examination Bulging hymen, abdominal mass, possible tenderness on pelvic examination Diagnostic Tests Pelvic ultrasound (shows collection of blood), MRI (detailed anatomy), examination under anesthesia Treatment Surgical intervention to remove the obstruction (hymenectomy, resection of septum) Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) (Option A) : Here an individual with a male karyotype (46, XY) cannot respond to androgens, resulting in female external genitalia despite the presence of testes and the absence of a uterus. MRKH syndrome (Option C) : A congenital disorder characterized by the absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina in females with normal ovarian function and secondary sexual characteristics. Asherman's syndrome (Option D) involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions or scar tissue. This condition can lead to secondary amenorrhea and infertility. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
resentation of cyclic abdominal pain, the absence of menarche, and the finding of a bulging, bluish hymen on physical examination are characteristics of an imperforate hymen causing cryptomenorrhea.
  • This condition leads to the accumulation of menstrual blood behind the hymen, which explains the distended vagina observed on ultrasound.
    • Cryptomenorrhea

    Definition

    Obstruction of menstrual blood outflow due to congenital malformations

    Common Causes

    Imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum, vaginal agenesis, cervical stenosis

    Symptoms/

    Complications

    Primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, abdominal mass, acute urinary retention, endometriosis, iatrogenic infections

    Physical Examination

    Bulging hymen, abdominal mass, possible tenderness on pelvic examination

    Diagnostic Tests

    Pelvic ultrasound (shows collection of blood), MRI (detailed anatomy), examination under anesthesia

    Treatment

    Surgical intervention to remove the obstruction (hymenectomy, resection of septum)

     

    Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) (Option A): Here an individual with a male karyotype (46, XY) cannot respond to androgens, resulting in female external genitalia despite the presence of testes and the absence of a uterus.
     

    MRKH syndrome (Option C): A congenital disorder characterized by the absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina in females with normal ovarian function and secondary sexual characteristics.


    Asherman's syndrome (Option D) involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions or scar tissue. This condition can lead to secondary amenorrhea and infertility.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old alcoholic patient presented to the OPD with atrophic scars and hyperpigmented lesions on the back of his hands, neck, face, and feet. Urine analysis revealed elevated uroporphyrin levels. On further evaluation, the patient was found to have a deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old alcoholic patient presented to the OPD with atrophic scars and hyperpigmented lesions on the back of his hands, neck, face, and feet. Urine analysis revealed elevated uroporphyrin levels. On further evaluation, the patient was found to have a deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: The image showing atrophic scars and hyperpigmented patches along with the uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase enzyme deficiency indicates that the likely diagnosis is Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT). It is the most common porphyria, has a complex inheritance pattern, and is of three types: Type I (sporadic) Type II (familial ) Type III The enzyme deficiency is acquired and restricted to hepatocytes due to the inhibition of a normal UROD enzyme. The enzyme deficiency is hereditary, present in all tissues, and associated with a UROD gene mutation. Rare type and is characterized by a hereditary enzyme deficiency localized to the liver. The major risk factors are subclinical genetic hemochromatosis, hepatitis C infection, alcohol , and estrogens. Patients exhibit increased fragility of light-exposed skin, presenting with painful bullae formation, subsequent crusting, and resulting in atrophic scarring, milia, and alterations in pigmentation, either hyper- or hypopigmentation. Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) can be defined by:

  • Very low weight-for-height/length (Z-score below -3SD).
  • A mid-upper arm circumference <115 mm.
  • The presence of nutritional oedema.

SAM significantly increases the risk of death in children under five years of age.

It can indirectly cause child death by increasing the case fatality rate in children suffering from common illnesses such as diarrhoea and pneumonia.

Children who are severely wasted (SAM) are 9 times more likely to die than well-nourished children.

MUAC >115 mm (Option A): SAM is defined by MUAC <115 mm, not above.

Weight-for-age Z-score below -1 SD (Option B): This is not used for SAM diagnosis. Weight-for-age < -2 SD defines underweight, not SAM.

Height-for-age Z-score below -2 SD (Option D): This defines stunting, a sign of chronic malnutrition, not acute malnutrition.

questions.solution: id="9cf83937931692777188a014337dcf">HEALING OF CORTICAL BONE: Stage of hematoma The initial stage lasts up to 7 days . Blood leaks from torn vessels and forms a hematoma around the fracture. The periosteum and soft tissues are stripped away from the fracture ends. Fracture ends suffer from ischemic necrosis over a few millimeters. Some osteocytes die, while others become active and help in healing. Stage of granulation tissue The granulation tissue stage lasts 2-3 weeks . Precursor cells produce blood vessels, fibroblasts, and osteoblasts. Soft granulation tissue forms between fracture fragments. It provides support without structural rigidity. A fibrous mesh from the blood clot supports fibroblast and capillary growth. Macrophages and giant cells remove the blood clot. In bone healing, granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts to form new bone. Stage of callus This stage lasts 4-12 weeks, during which granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts. These cells create an intercellular matrix that becomes impregnated with calcium salts, forming the callus, or woven bone. This callus, visible on X-rays about 3 weeks post-fracture, provides initial strength and indicates union. Stage of remodeling Formerly known as the consolidation stage. Woven bone is replaced by mature lamellar bone. This occurs in multicellular units, with callus replaced by lamellar bone. The process is slow, taking 1 to 4 years. Stage of modeling Formerly known as the remodeling stage. Bone is gradually strengthened. Cortices sharpen at the endosteal and periosteal surfaces. Local bone strains from weight-bearing stresses and muscle forces stimulate this process. More noticeable in children with angulated fractures. Limited remodeling occurs in adult fractures. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
id="9cf83937931692777188a014337dcf">HEALING OF CORTICAL BONE:

 

Stage of hematoma
  • The initial stage lasts up to 7 days.
  • Blood leaks from torn vessels and forms a hematoma around the fracture.
  • The periosteum and soft tissues are stripped away from the fracture ends.
  • Fracture ends suffer from ischemic necrosis over a few millimeters.
  • Some osteocytes die, while others become active and help in healing.

Stage of granulation tissue
  • The granulation tissue stage lasts 2-3 weeks.
  • Precursor cells produce blood vessels, fibroblasts, and osteoblasts.
  • Soft granulation tissue forms between fracture fragments.
  • It provides support without structural rigidity.
  • A fibrous mesh from the blood clot supports fibroblast and capillary growth.
  • Macrophages and giant cells remove the blood clot.
  • In bone healing, granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts to form new bone.

Stage of callus
  • This stage lasts 4-12 weeks, during which granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts.
  • These cells create an intercellular matrix that becomes impregnated with calcium salts, forming the callus, or woven bone.
  • This callus, visible on X-rays about 3 weeks post-fracture, provides initial strength and indicates union.

Stage of remodeling

  • Formerly known as the consolidation stage.
  • Woven bone is replaced by mature lamellar bone.
  • This occurs in multicellular units, with callus replaced by lamellar bone.
  • The process is slow, taking 1 to 4 years.

Stage of modeling

  • Formerly known as the remodeling stage.
  • Bone is gradually strengthened.
  • Cortices sharpen at the endosteal and periosteal surfaces.
  • Local bone strains from weight-bearing stresses and muscle forces stimulate this process.
  • More noticeable in children with angulated fractures.
  • Limited remodeling occurs in adult fractures.

questions.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl presents with persistent crying, refusal to eat, and multiple bruises. The parents report frequent falls. On exam, there are bruises on the abdomen and back, a healing burn on the thigh, and rib tenderness. X-ray done is shown below. The parents give vague explanations and claim the child "bruises easily." A CT scan reveals subdural hematoma without a clear trauma history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: or Battered Baby Syndrome is strongly suggested when a child presents with multiple injuries at different stages of healing, and the parents provide a vague or inconsistent explanation. The rib fractures, bruises, and a healing burn- combined with intracranial hemorrhage without significant trauma- point to ongoing physical abuse. Battered Baby Syndrome (Caffey-Kempe Syndrome): A battered child is one who has sustained repeated physical harm due to intentional violence inflicted by a parent or guardian. Other names include Caffey-Kempe syndrome , maltreatment syndrome , or parent-infant traumatic stress syndrome . Features Raising Suspicion of Abuse: Inconsistent History : Parents may provide vague explanations for injuries, such as a fall, which do not match the type or timing of the injuries. Delayed Medical Care : Parents often seek medical help only when the child’s condition worsens. Injuries in Various Stages : Multiple injuries at different healing stages are often present. Parental Admission : Parents may later confess to mild punishment but downplay the severity. Injuries: Surface Injuries : Bruises, abrasions, and lacerations, including characteristic labial frenulum tears. CNS Injuries : Encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and subdural hematoma (SDH), indicative of shaken baby syndrome. Eye Injuries : Retinal hemorrhages and possible lens dislocation. Visceral Injuries : Damage to the spleen, liver, or intestines. Burns : Cigarette burns or scalds from hot liquids are often found. Skeletal Injuries : Fractures (transverse, spiral, metaphyseal chip fractures), rib fractures, and the characteristic "string of beads" appearance on X-rays are common. Cardiovascular Injuries : Rib fractures, lung and heart contusions. Genitourinary Injuries : Consider sexual abuse. Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A) : Causes frequent fractures but does not account for bruising, burns, or intracranial hemorrhage. Munchausen syndrome by proxy (Option C) : Involves a caregiver fabricating or inducing illness in a child, but the repeated physical injuries in this case make direct physical abuse more likely. Hemophilia (Option D) : Could explain bruising but not the presence of fractures and burn marks. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: on: Valproate increases GABA levels by inhibiting GABA transaminase , which breaks down GABA, and Succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, which is involved in the GABA degradation pathway. Mechanism of Action of Valproate Sodium Channel Inactivation : Prolongs Na+ channel inactivation in a frequency-dependent manner, similar to phenytoin. Calcium Channel Modulatio n: Weakly attenuates the T-type calcium currents, akin to ethosuximide. GABA Enhancement : Increases GABA levels by: Inhibiting GABA transaminase, leading to reduced degradation. Possibly enhancing GABA synthesis from glutamic acid. Glutamate Receptor Blockade : Blocks excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors, reducing excitatory neurotransmission. GABA decarboxylase and Glutamate decarboxylase (Option B) : These enzymes are involved in the synthesis of GABA, not its degradation. GABA transaminase and Glutamate dehydrogenase (Option C): Glutamate dehydrogenase is not directly involved in the GABA metabolic pathway. on:

Valproate increases GABA levels by inhibiting GABA transaminase, which breaks down GABA, and Succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, which is involved in the GABA degradation pathway.


 

Mechanism of Action of Valproate

  • Sodium Channel Inactivation: Prolongs Na+ channel inactivation in a frequency-dependent manner, similar to phenytoin.
  • Calcium Channel Modulation: Weakly attenuates the T-type calcium currents, akin to ethosuximide.
  • GABA Enhancement: Increases GABA levels by:
    • Inhibiting GABA transaminase, leading to reduced degradation.
    • Possibly enhancing GABA synthesis from glutamic acid.
  • Glutamate Receptor Blockade: Blocks excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors, reducing excitatory neurotransmission.

GABA decarboxylase and Glutamate decarboxylase (Option B) : These enzymes are involved in the synthesis of GABA, not its degradation.

GABA transaminase and Glutamate dehydrogenase (Option C): Glutamate dehydrogenase is not directly involved in the GABA metabolic pathway.

Glutamate decarboxylase and Succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (Option D): Glutamate decarboxylase is involved in GABA synthesis, not degradation.

questions.solution: with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test , which detects heterophile IgM antibodies . These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells —a hallmark of EBV infection. Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests: Weil-Felix : Rickettsial infections Paul-Bunnell : Infectious mononucleosis Cold agglutination : Mycoplasma pneumonia Streptococcus MG : Streptococcal antibodies Paul-Bunnell Test Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV. Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum. Principle : Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections Procedure : Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs Interpretation : Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection Note : Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs @Neet_pg_bot

with fever, sore throat, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly is classic for infectious mononucleosis (IM) caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

  • Diagnosis is supported by the Paul–Bunnell (Monospot) test, which detects heterophile IgM antibodies. These antibodies are non-specific and can agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells—a hallmark of EBV infection.

    • Examples of Heterophile Antigen Tests:

    • Weil-Felix: Rickettsial infections

    • Paul-Bunnell: Infectious mononucleosis

    • Cold agglutination: Mycoplasma pneumonia

    • Streptococcus MG: Streptococcal antibodies

    Paul-Bunnell Test

    • Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV.
    • Utilizes sheep RBCs as antigens to detect heterophile antibodies in the patient’s serum.

    • Principle: Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep RBCs; can occur rarely in normal individuals or after serum injections

    • Procedure: Heat serum (56°C, 30 min), mix with 1% sheep RBCs in doubling dilutions, incubate 37°C for 4 hrs

    • Interpretation: Agglutination titer ≥100 → suggests infection

    • Note: Paul-Bunnell → sheep RBCs; Monospot → horse RBCs

questions.solution: The MRI findings suggest Von Meyenberg complexes (VMCs), which are small, typically asymptomatic lesions in the liver resulting from ductal plate malformations. They are often discovered incidentally during imaging and can be associated with conditions like autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Von Meyenberg complex (Bile Duct Microhamartomas) Small (<1.5 cm), usually multiple greyish nodular lesions in the liver due to ductal plate malformations. Associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Caroli's disease, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. (Option C ruled out) MRI/MRCP: Multiple irregularly delineated hyper-intense cystic nodules, not communicating with the biliary tree. Gadolinium contrast enhances differentiation from Caroli's disease. Rare malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma. (Option A ruled out) VMCs are rare liver findings with distinct MRI features. questions.solutionHtml:
The MRI findings suggest Von Meyenberg complexes (VMCs), which are small, typically asymptomatic lesions in the liver resulting from ductal plate malformations. They are often discovered incidentally during imaging and can be associated with conditions like autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

 

Von Meyenberg complex (Bile Duct Microhamartomas)

  • Small (<1.5 cm), usually multiple greyish nodular lesions in the liver due to ductal plate malformations.
  • Associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Caroli's disease, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. (Option D ruled out)
  • Histology: Cystically dilated bile ducts lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium in a collagenous stroma.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Generally asymptomatic; Incidental findings during laparoscopic procedures or autopsies.
    • Can present with non-specific abdominal discomfort or episodes of cholangitis.
  • Imaging Modalities and Findings
    • Ultrasound: Multiple hyper- or hypoechoic areas with comet tail echoes.
    • CT Scan: Multiple irregular small low-attenuated areas, typically without enhancement on contrast injection. (Option C ruled out)
    • MRI/MRCP: Multiple irregularly delineated hyper-intense cystic nodules, not communicating with the biliary tree. Gadolinium contrast enhances differentiation from Caroli's disease.
  • Rare malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma. (Option A ruled out)
  • VMCs are rare liver findings with distinct MRI features. They typically cause no symptoms but can occasionally lead to abdominal discomfort or liver infections.

questions.solution: The scenario is indicative of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) , in which the blockage of D2 receptors leads to extrapyramidal side effects, and the drug of choice for treatment is Dantrolene sodium. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Description A rare, potentially fatal consequence of neuroleptic administration. Mechanism D2 receptor blocking at: Striatum (muscle rigidity) Hypothalamus (hyperthermia) Spinal nerves (autonomic disturbances) Clinical manifestations Motor and behavioural Autonomic symptoms Muscular rigidity (most common) Dystonia Akinesia, Mutism Obtundation Agitation Fever (most common) Diaphoresis Raised pulse and blood pressure Sweating Altered consciousness Associated conditions Renal failure and myoglobinuria Laboratory findings Raised levels of creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) (most common) Leukocytosis (raised WBC) Raised liver enzymes Raised plasma myoglobin Management Stop the drug (causing symptoms) Supportive care (maintain hydration and other vitals) Skeletal muscle relaxants: Dantrolene sodium (drug of choice) Dopamine agonists: Bromocriptine, Amantadine Second-generation antipsychotics (for restarting the treatment for Schizophrenia). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The scenario is indicative of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), in which the blockage of D2 receptors leads to extrapyramidal side effects, and the drug of choice for treatment is Dantrolene sodium.

 

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

Description

A rare, potentially fatal consequence of neuroleptic administration.

Mechanism

D2 receptor blocking at:

  • Striatum (muscle rigidity)
  • Hypothalamus (hyperthermia)
  • Spinal nerves (autonomic disturbances)
 

Clinical manifestations

Motor and behavioural

Autonomic symptoms
  • Muscular rigidity (most common)
  • Dystonia
  • Akinesia,
  • Mutism
  • Obtundation
  • Agitation
  • Fever (most common)
  • Diaphoresis
  • Raised pulse and blood pressure
  • Sweating
  • Altered consciousness

Associated conditions

Renal failure and myoglobinuria

Laboratory findings
  • Raised levels of creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) (most common)
  • Leukocytosis (raised WBC)
  • Raised liver enzymes
  • Raised plasma myoglobin

Management

  • Stop the drug (causing symptoms)
  • Supportive care (maintain hydration and other vitals)
  • Skeletal muscle relaxants: Dantrolene sodium (drug of choice)
  • Dopamine agonists: Bromocriptine, Amantadine
  • Second-generation antipsychotics (for restarting the treatment for Schizophrenia).

In scurvy, you would see characteristic lines such as the White Line of Frankel (Dense lines between epiphysis and metaphysis) and a ground glass appearance in the bones, indicating abnormal mineralization. X-ray Findings of Scurvy Characteristic Lines: Specific radiological lines indicative of scurvy are observed. White Line of Frankel: Dense line between epiphysis and metaphysis. Due to calcification. Scurvy Line: Dense line within the metaphysis. Weinberger’s Ring Line: Dense line within the epiphysis. strong>

The child's symptoms of leg pain, swollen gums, irritability, and subcutaneous bruising, combined with the suspicion of vitamin deficiency, suggest a diagnosis of scurvy.

In scurvy, you would see characteristic lines such as the White Line of Frankel (Dense lines between epiphysis and metaphysis) and a ground glass appearance in the bones, indicating abnormal mineralization.

 

X-ray Findings of Scurvy

  1. Characteristic Lines: Specific radiological lines indicative of scurvy are observed.
    • White Line of Frankel: Dense line between epiphysis and metaphysis. Due to calcification.
    • Scurvy Line: Dense line within the metaphysis.
    • Weinberger’s Ring Line: Dense line within the epiphysis.
  2. Trümmerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line
  3. Pelkan Spurs: Bone spurs from the lateral border of the metaphysis.
  4. Ground Glass Appearance of the bones.
  5. Subperiosteal Fractures: Fractures may occur beneath the periosteum.
  6. Epiphyseal Fracture Separation.

Normal bone structure (Option A): This is unlikely given the symptoms of pain, swelling, and bruising. Vitamin deficiencies typically lead to identifiable changes in bone structure on X-rays.

 

Widened epiphyseal plates and cupping of the metaphysis (Option C): This is associated with rickets but does not reflect the expected "dense lines" seen with vitamin D deficiency.

 

Increased bone density with no fractures (Option D): This is more typical of conditions like osteopetrosis or other metabolic bone disorders, not vitamin D deficiency, which typically leads to decreased bone mineralization and associated symptoms.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the activation mechanism of transmembrane guanylyl cyclases (pGCs)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes the activation mechanism of transmembrane guanylyl cyclases (pGCs)?

options.label: A
options.text: Ligand binding induces a conformational change, activating cGMP synthesis.

options.label: C
options.text: The intracellular domain initiates gene transcription.

options.label: D
options.text: Intracellular proteins bind to activate cGMP synthesis.

questions.answerText: Ligand binding induces a conformational change, activating cGMP synthesis.
questions.solution: Correct answer A)Ligand binding induces a conformational change, activating cGMP synthesis. Ligand binding to the extracellular domain causes a conformational change that activates the cyclase domains, leading to cGMP synthesis. B) Phosphorylation within the kinase homology domain (KHD) is important but does not directly activate cGMP synthesis; ligand-induced conformational change is the primary mechanism. C) The intracellular domains of pGCs do not bind to DNA or initiate gene transcription; they are involved in cGMP synthesis. D) While some pGCs are regulated by intracellular proteins, the primary activation mechanism for most pGCs involves ligand binding to the extracellular domain. Guanylyl Cyclase Receptor: Transmembrane guanylyl cyclases (pGCs) are homodimers (~1,050 amino acids each). Composed of a short transmembrane domain (21-25 hydrophobic amino acids) separating extracellular and intracellular regions. Extracellular domain acts as a receptor for specific peptide hormones. Domains: Extracellular Domain: Binds specific ligands. Juxtamembranous Protein Kinase-Homology Domain (KHD): ~250 residues, lacks kinase activity. Cyclase Domain: Catalytic region for cGMP formation at the COOH-terminal end. Activation Mechanism: Ligand Binding: Specific ligands (e.g., ANP) bind, causing a conformational change. Conformational Change: Rotation within the dimer activates cGMP synthesis by approximating cyclase domains . Phosphorylation: Activation is modulated by phosphorylation in the KHD; ligand binding may expose phosphorylated sites to phosphatases for dephosphorylation and inactivation. Desensitization: Prolonged ligand exposure can lead to dephosphorylation of the KHD, reducing pGC activity. Intracellular Signalling: cGMP Production: Activated cyclase domain produces cGMP from GTP, serving as a second messenger. cGMP Targets: cGMP-Dependent Protein Kinases (cGKs): Phosphorylate proteins to elicit cellular responses. Phosphodiesterases (PDEs): Regulate cGMP levels by hydrolyzing it . cGMP-Gated Channels: Involved in phototransduction and olfactory signaling @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer A)Ligand binding induces a conformational change, activating cGMP synthesis.

Ligand binding to the extracellular domain causes a conformational change that activates the cyclase domains, leading to cGMP synthesis.

B) Phosphorylation within the kinase homology domain (KHD) is important but does not directly activate cGMP synthesis; ligand-induced conformational change is the primary mechanism.

C) The intracellular domains of pGCs do not bind to DNA or initiate gene transcription; they are involved in cGMP synthesis.

D) While some pGCs are regulated by intracellular proteins, the primary activation mechanism for most pGCs involves ligand binding to the extracellular domain.

Guanylyl Cyclase Receptor:

  • Transmembrane guanylyl cyclases (pGCs) are homodimers (~1,050 amino acids each).
  • Composed of a short transmembrane domain (21-25 hydrophobic amino acids) separating extracellular and intracellular regions.
  • Extracellular domain acts as a receptor for specific peptide hormones.

Domains:

  • Extracellular Domain: Binds specific ligands.
  • Juxtamembranous Protein Kinase-Homology Domain (KHD): ~250 residues, lacks kinase activity.
  • Cyclase Domain: Catalytic region for cGMP formation at the COOH-terminal end.

Activation Mechanism:

  • Ligand Binding: Specific ligands (e.g., ANP) bind, causing a conformational change.
  • Conformational Change: Rotation within the dimer activates cGMP synthesis by approximating cyclase domains.
  • Phosphorylation: Activation is modulated by phosphorylation in the KHD; ligand binding may expose phosphorylated sites to phosphatases for dephosphorylation and inactivation.
  • Desensitization: Prolonged ligand exposure can lead to dephosphorylation of the KHD, reducing pGC activity.

Intracellular Signalling:

  • cGMP Production: Activated cyclase domain produces cGMP from GTP, serving as a second messenger.
  • cGMP Targets:
    • cGMP-Dependent Protein Kinases (cGKs): Phosphorylate proteins to elicit cellular responses.
    • Phosphodiesterases (PDEs): Regulate cGMP levels by hydrolyzing it.
    • cGMP-Gated Channels: Involved in phototransduction and olfactory signaling

questions.solution: 93cfd480f228">mutation Explanation: Hirschsprung’s disease (Aganglionic megacolon): It is due to congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in both myentric and meissner’s plexus in segment of distal colon due to failure of cranial to caudal migration of neural crest cells during development. Causes: Endothelial B receptor gene mutation. Neural crest cell migration defect. RET proto-oncogene mutation. Symptoms : Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life. Abdominal distention. Bilious vomiting. Constipation. Failure to thrive. Clinical Features : Lack of stool in the rectal vault on digital rectal examination. Explosive release of gas and stool upon withdrawal of the examining finger (squirt sign). Chronic constipation in older children. Meconium ileus (Option A ruled out) : Associated with cystic fibrosis . Usually involves obstruction in the distal ileum (not colon). X-ray: "Soap-bubble" appearance . NOT typically associated with a narrowed distal colon Increased enteric ganglion cells (Option B ruled out) : This would enhance motility , not cause obstruction. In Hirschsprung, the issue is lack of ganglion cells. Intestinal atresia (Option C ruled out) : Usually presents with double bubble or triple bubble sign on X-ray, depending on location (duodenal, jejunal, etc.). Often has polyhydramnios in utero. Not typically associated with transition zone in colon @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
93cfd480f228">mutation

Explanation:

Hirschsprung’s disease (Aganglionic megacolon):

It is due to congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in both myentric and meissner’s plexus in segment of distal colon due to failure of cranial to caudal migration of neural crest cells during development.

Causes:

  • Endothelial B receptor gene mutation.
  • Neural crest cell migration defect.
  • RET proto-oncogene mutation.

Symptoms:

  • Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life.
  • Abdominal distention.
  • Bilious vomiting.
  • Constipation.
  • Failure to thrive.

Clinical Features:

  • Lack of stool in the rectal vault on digital rectal examination.
  • Explosive release of gas and stool upon withdrawal of the examining finger (squirt sign).
  • Chronic constipation in older children.

 

Meconium ileus (Option A ruled out): Associated with cystic fibrosis. Usually involves obstruction in the distal ileum (not colon). X-ray: "Soap-bubble" appearance. NOT typically associated with a narrowed distal colon

Increased enteric ganglion cells (Option B ruled out): This would enhance motility, not cause obstruction. In Hirschsprung, the issue is lack of ganglion cells.

Intestinal atresia (Option   C ruled out): Usually presents with double bubble or triple bubble sign on X-ray, depending on location (duodenal, jejunal, etc.). Often has polyhydramnios in utero. Not typically associated with transition zone in colon

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent respiratory infections and poor growth despite a normal diet. Genetic testing reveals Cystic fibrosis. What type of mutation causes cystic fibrosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent respiratory infections and poor growth despite a normal diet. Genetic testing reveals Cystic fibrosis. What type of mutation causes cystic fibrosis?
questions.solution: Correct answer C) Allelic heterogeneity Allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations within the same gene causing the same disease . In cystic fibrosis, many different mutations in the CFTR gene can cause the disease Phenotypic heterogeneity (Option A ruled out) Pleiotropy (Option B ruled out) Allelic heterogeneity (Option C) Variability in the phenotype that is caused by mutations in the same gene Disorders where multiple, seemingly unrelated organ systems are affected. A single gene is responsible for several distinct and seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects Different mutations (changes) in a single gene cause the same disease or condition Example: Loss-of-function mutations in the RET gene, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase, leads to inherited failure of development of colonic ganglia, leading to defective colonic motility and severe chronic constipation (Hirschsprung disease) Example: The allele causing neurofibromatosis type 1 can produce abnormalities of skin pigmentation, neurofibromas of the peripheral nerves, short stature, macrocephaly, skeletal abnormalities, and fits Example: Cystic fibrosis is caused by having one of many different mutations in the CFTR gene. Heteroplasmy (Option D) refers to the presence of more than one type of mitochondrial DNA within a cell or individual. This is not relevant to cystic fibrosis, which is caused by mutations in the nuclear CFTR gene, not mitochondrial DNA @Neet_pg_bot

  • Disorders where multiple, seemingly unrelated organ systems are affected.

Different mutations (changes) in a single gene cause the same disease or condition

Example:

Loss-of-function mutations in the RET gene, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase, leads to inherited failure of development of colonic ganglia, leading to defective colonic motility and severe chronic constipation (Hirschsprung disease)

Example:

questions.solution: ent's symptoms suggest nerve root compression, commonly caused by a herniated disc. The key findings in this case include lower back pain radiating down the left leg, numbness over the top of the foot, and weakness in dorsiflexion of the great toe (extensor hallucis longus), without reflex abnormalities. These are classic signs of L5 nerve root involvement. L5 nerve root compression, often due to L4-L5 disc herniation, results in: Weakness in great toe dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus). Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Radiating pain down the lateral aspect of leg. Slipped disc: A herniated disc, also known as a slipped disc, occurs when the soft center (nucleus pulposus) of a spinal disc pushes through a tear in the tougher exterior (annulus fibrosus) and presses on nearby nerves. Herniated discs most commonly occur in the cervical (neck) and lumbar (lower back) spine. Here's an explanation of herniated discs affecting both the cervical and lumbar regions. Cervical Slip Disc (Upper Limb Involvement): In the cervical region, the nerves exit above their corresponding vertebrae (except for the C8 nerve). The affected nerve root, in the case of a herniated disc, is typically the one corresponding to the lower vertebra in the pair. Cervical Slip Discs and Affected Nerve Roots Herniated Disc Between Compressed Nerve Root Symptoms (Upper Limb) C4 and C5 C5 Shoulder pain, weakness in deltoid muscle C5 and C6 C6 Pain in biceps, weakness in wrist extension C6 and C7 C7 Triceps weakness, difficulty extending the elbow C7 and T1 C8 Hand weakness, difficulty with finger movements Lumbar Slip Disc (Lower Limb Involvement) In the lumbar region, the nerves exit below their corresponding vertebrae. Therefore, when a disc herniation occurs between two vertebrae, the nerve root corresponding to the lower vertebra is usually compressed. Lumbar Slip Discs and Affected Nerve Roots Herniated Disc Between Compressed Nerve Root Symptoms (Lower Limb) L3 and L4 L4 Weakness in knee extension, reduced patellar reflex L4 and L5 L5 Weakness in foot dorsiflexion, difficulty walking L5 and S1 S1 Pain down the back of the leg, reduced Achilles reflex, foot drop Regional Prevalence: Cervicothoracic (C6-T1): 10% of cases Lumbosacral (L4-S1): 90% of cases Thoracic: Rare L3-L4 (Option A): Compression at this level typically affects the L4 nerve root, causing weakness in knee extension (quadriceps) and decreased sensation over the medial side of the lower leg. This is not consistent with the patient's symptoms. L5-S1 (Option C): Compression here would affect the S1 nerve root, causing weakness in plantarflexion (gastrocnemius), decreased ankle reflex, and sensory loss along the lateral aspect of the foot. This does not match the patient's findings. questions.stemHtml: A newborn is diagnosed with a condition where their haemoglobin has an unusually high affinity for oxygen. What is the physiological basis for the increased oxygen affinity of fetal haemoglobin compared to adult haemoglobin?

options.label: B
options.text: HbF contains serine that reduces the positive charge of the globin side chain.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher histidine content, reducing oxygen affinity.

options.label: D
options.text: Binds oxygen more loosely than adult Hb

questions.answerText: HbF contains serine that reduces the positive charge of the globin side chain.
questions.solution: Correct answer B) HbF contains serine that reduces the positive charge of the globin side chain. Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) contains α₂ and γ₂ globin chains, where γ chains have serine instead of histidine. (Beta chains have more of histidine and lysine). This reduces the positive charge in the heme’s central cavity, leading to decreased binding of 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). Difference between Adult Hemoglobin and Fetal Hemoglobin” Feature Adult Hemoglobin (HbA) Fetal Hemoglobin (HbF) Globin Side Chains α₂β₂ α₂γ₂ Oxygen Affinity Lower Higher 2,3-BPG Binding Higher Lower Physiological Role Tissue oxygen delivery Oxygen extraction from maternal blood Charge in Central Cavity More positive Less positive pH Sensitivity More sensitive Less sensitive Binds more 2,3-BPG, increasing oxygen affinity (Option A): Incorrect- More 2,3-BPG binding decreases oxygen affinity , stabilizing the taut form. HbF binds less 2,3-BPG , increasing its affinity for oxygen. Higher histidine content, reducing oxygen affinity (Option C): Incorrect- HbF has serine instead of histidine in its γ-chain, which actually increases oxygen affinity. Binds oxygen more loosely than adult Hb (Option D): Incorrect - HbF binds oxygen more tightly than HbA to facilitate oxygen transfer from maternal blood. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following statements regarding elimination characteristics of "hit and run" drugs are incorrect?
	These drugs are eliminated quickly and have short half-lives.
	These drugs produce a prolonged effect even after they are eliminated from the body.
	These drugs require continuous administration to maintain their therapeutic effect.
	Omeprazole and reserpine are classified under these drugs.
	Regular blood samples are needed to monitor plasma concentration.
questions.solution: ; Explanation: Hit-and-run drugs are not defined by their rate of elimination, do not require continuous administration, and monitoring of plasma concentration has no value. Hit and Run drugs: Create lasting effects by irreversibly binding to targets, initiating a cascade that persists even after the drug is eliminated (Statement 2). The effect lasts much longer than the drug itself. Do not require continuous administration due to prolonged effect. Plasma concentration monitoring is of no value. Examples include reserpine, guanethidine, MAO inhibitors, and omeprazole (Statement 4). @Neet_pg_bot

After 48 hours, he develops severe hypoxemia with PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 110, bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray, and no signs of left heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male is admitted to the ICU after sustaining blunt chest trauma in a motor vehicle accident. Chest imaging reveals pulmonary contusions. After 48 hours, he develops severe hypoxemia with PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 110, bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray, and no signs of left heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Insert a wide-bore needle in the fifth intercostal space

options.label: B
options.text: Start intravenous furosemide to reduce pulmonary edema

options.label: C
options.text: Begin low tidal volume mechanical ventilation

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy

questions.answerText: Begin low tidal volume mechanical ventilation
questions.solution: Answer is C: Low volume ventilation This patient has developed ARDS, likely secondary to pulmonary contusion, confirmed by bilateral infiltrates and low PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio. The cornerstone of ARDS management is lung-protective ventilation using low tidal volumes (4–6 mL/kg of predicted body weight) to prevent volutrauma and barotrauma. Option A (wide-bore needle) is used for tension pneumothorax, which would present with absent breath sounds and hemodynamic compromise, not diffuse infiltrates. Option B (Lasix) may be harmful here , as ARDS is due to inflammatory alveolar damage, not fluid overload. Option D (HFNC) is insufficient in moderate-to-severe ARDS, where invasive ventilation is required to maintain oxygenation and protect lungs. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Answer is C: Low volume ventilation 

This patient has developed ARDS, likely secondary to pulmonary contusion, confirmed by bilateral infiltrates and low PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio. The cornerstone of ARDS management is lung-protective ventilation using low tidal volumes (4–6 mL/kg of predicted body weight) to prevent volutrauma and barotrauma. Option A (wide-bore needle) is used for tension pneumothorax, which would present with absent breath sounds and hemodynamic compromise, not diffuse infiltrates. Option B (Lasix) may be harmful here, as ARDS is due to inflammatory alveolar damage, not fluid overload. Option D (HFNC) is insufficient in moderate-to-severe ARDS, where invasive ventilation is required to maintain oxygenation and protect lungs.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman’s transvaginal ultrasound reveals a 5 cm ectopic pregnancy located in the ampulla of the right fallopian tube. The initial serum beta hCG level was 3500 IU/L and has remained stable despite receiving three doses of methotrexate. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
questions.solution: ng> Explanation: This patient has an unruptured ectopic pregnancy in the right fallopian tube that has failed to respond to medical management with methotrexate. Laparoscopic salpingectomy involves the removal of the affected fallopian tube . It is indicated when medical therapy fails or is contraindicated, such as in cases of larger ectopic pregnancies (> 4 cm) or persistent beta hCG levels. Expectant management (Option A) involves observation of the patient, hoping for spontaneous resolution. This is a viable option in cases where the beta hCG level is low or falling. Hysterectomy (Option B) is not considered a management option for ectopic pregnancy. Laparoscopic linear salpingostomy (Option C) is done only in H/O infertility or if the unaffected tube is also looking unhealthy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
n:

The scenario here points to the diagnosis of laryngomalacia, which presents with a stridor that increases on crying and an omega-shaped glottis on laryngoscopy.

 

Laryngomalacia or Congenital Laryngeal Stridor

  • Most common congenital abnormality of the larynx.
  • During inspiration, an excessively flaccid supraglottic larynx gets sucked in and causes the symptoms.

Clinical Features
  • Presents at birth or immediately after
  • Stridor:
    • Increases on crying (increased negative intrathoracic pressure pulls the epiglottis inward, covering the laryngeal inlet)
    • Stridor present in supine position (as the epiglottis covers the laryngeal inlet)
    • Subsides in prone position (as the epiglottis falls away from the larynx)
  • Cyanosis seen sometimes
  • Normal cry
  • Usually disappears by 2 years of age

Investigations
  • Direct laryngoscopy:
    • Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself giving an “omega-shaped” appearance.
    • Floppy aryepiglottic folds
    • Prominent aretynoids
  • Flexible laryngoscopy is the most preferred

Management
  • Conservative treatment in most cases
  • Tracheostomy: If severe respiratory obstruction
  • Supraglottoplasty: If severe laryngomalacia


 

Congenital subglottic stenosis (Option A) is a congenital condition where there is an abnormal thickening of the cricoid cartilage or fibrous tissue below the vocal cords. It may be asymptomatic until upper respiratory tract infections lead to dyspnoea and stridor. The cry is normal.

 

Subglottic hemangioma (Option B) is also a congenital condition but presents only by 3-6 months of age as hemangioma grows in size and causes stridor. Agitation and crying may increase the obstruction.

 

Laryngeal web (Option C) is caused due to incomplete recanalization of the larynx and presents with airway obstruction, weak cry, or aphonia from birth.

>
  • T1a stage indicates that the tumor was found incidentally during a procedure like TURP and involves less than 5% of the resected tissue. The tumor is usually well-differentiated.

    •  

    TNM Staging System for Prostate Cancer

    • T1: Incidentally found tumors in a clinically benign gland.
      • T1a: Tumor involves <5% of the resected specimen. (Option A)
      • T1b: Tumor involves >5% of the resected specimen. (Option B ruled out)
      • T1c: Impalpable tumor found due to raised PSA.
    • T2: Tumor confined within the prostate capsule.
      • T2a: Involves one lobe. (Option C ruled out)
      • T2b: Involves more than half of one side but not both sides.
      • T2c: Involves both sides, confined within the capsule.
    • T3: Tumor extends through the capsule.
      • T3a: Unilateral or bilateral extension. (Option D ruled out)
      • T3b: Extension into seminal vesicles.
    • T4: Tumor invades adjacent structures (e.g., levator muscles, external sphincter, rectum, pelvic sidewall).
    • N0: No regional lymph node involvement
    • N1: Regional lymph node involvement
    • M0: No distant metastasis
    • M1: Distant metastasis present

questions.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old male presents with a sudden onset of severe fatigue, weakness, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. On examination, he is hypotensive (BP 75/45 mmHg), tachycardic (HR 115 bpm), and has noticeable diffuse skin hyperpigmentation, especially in sun-exposed areas and palmar creases. Laboratory results reveal:
	Sodium: 128 mEq/L
	Potassium: 5.8 mEq/L
	Glucose: 58 mg/dL
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: > Addison's disease , or primary adrenal insufficiency , is characterized by the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to deficient production of cortisol and aldosterone. In an acute crisis, patients present with severe hypotension, electrolyte imbalances (low sodium, high potassium), hypoglycemia, and dehydration, which are all seen in this patient. Diffuse skin hyperpigmentation occurs due to increased ACTH levels stimulating melanocytes, which is a hallmark of Addison's disease. Diabetic ketoacidosis (Option A) typically presents with hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia. The electrolyte pattern and skin hyperpigmentation are not consistent with DKA. Septic shock (Option B) can cause hypotension and tachycardia, but doesn't explain electrolyte abnormalities, or skin hyperpigmentation. Septic shock typically causes hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia. Panhypopituitarism (Option D) can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency, but it wouldn't result in skin hyperpigmentation (due to low ACTH levels). Also, the electrolyte abnormalities are typically less severe in secondary adrenal insufficiency because aldosterone production is usually preserved. @Neet_pg_bot

>Addison's disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, is characterized by the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to deficient production of cortisol and aldosterone.
  • In an acute crisis, patients present with severe hypotension, electrolyte imbalances (low sodium, high potassium), hypoglycemia, and dehydration, which are all seen in this patient.
  • Diffuse skin hyperpigmentation occurs due to increased ACTH levels stimulating melanocytes, which is a hallmark of Addison's disease.

    • Diabetic ketoacidosis (Option A) typically presents with hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia.

    • The electrolyte pattern and skin hyperpigmentation are not consistent with DKA.

     

    Septic shock (Option B) can cause hypotension and tachycardia, but doesn't explain electrolyte abnormalities, or skin hyperpigmentation.

    • Septic shock typically causes hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia.

     

    Panhypopituitarism (Option D) can cause secondary adrenal insufficiency, but it wouldn't result in skin hyperpigmentation (due to low ACTH levels).

    • Also, the electrolyte abnormalities are typically less severe in secondary adrenal insufficiency because aldosterone production is usually preserved.

Radiological Examination for CSF Rhinorrhea

 

High-Resolution CT(HRCT)
  • Investigation of choice for identifying skull base defects.
  • 3D reconstruction helps evaluate congenital or spontaneous defects.
  • Useful for detecting trauma, developmental abnormalities, or erosive lesions.

CT Cisternography
  • Involves intrathecal contrast injection to localize the CSF leak.
  • Improves diagnostic yield, especially in active leaks.
  • May miss cribriform or ethmoid sinus defects.
  • Invasive procedure with potential side effects like nausea and headaches.

MRI (Option B)
  • Not first-line unless encephalocele is suspected.
  • Less effective for identifying bony defects compared to CT.
  • More costly and time-consuming; and may require a contrast agent.









 

CT cisternography(Option C) involves intrathecal contrast and is more invasive, reserved for difficult cases when the leak site isn't found by HRCT.

X-ray of the skull(Option D) has limited value in detecting CSF leaks or skull base defects.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a rapidly growing 3 cm mass in his right cheek. Biopsy shows small round blue cells, alveolar patterns, eosinophilic cytoplasm with cross-striations, and positive immunochemistry for desmin and myogenin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has a rapidly growing 3 cm mass in his right cheek. Biopsy shows small round blue cells, alveolar patterns, eosinophilic cytoplasm with cross-striations, and positive immunochemistry for desmin and myogenin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Explanation: The clinical presentation and histopathology features suggest Rhabdomyosarcoma , a malignant tumour that arises from primitive mesenchymal cells committed to the skeletal muscle lineage. It is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents. It can occur anywhere in the body, but common sites include the head and neck, genitourinary tract, and extremities. It typically presents as a painless, rapidly growing mass, often in the head and neck region. Histopathology reveals small round blue cells with features of skeletal muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry confirms the diagnosis with positive for muscle markers like desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1. Treatment involves a multimodal approach, including surgery, chemotherapy, and often radiation therapy. Prognosis varies widely depending on subtype, location, stage, and age at diagnosis. Ewing Sarcoma (Option A) typically presents with small, round blue cells with scant cytoplasm lacking muscle differentiation. It commonly affects bone or soft tissue in children and young adults and is often associated with the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion gene. Neuroblastoma (Option B) usually originates from the adrenal gland or sympathetic ganglia in young children. Histology reveals small, round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes and neurite-like processes, positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. Lymphoma (Option D) typically shows monomorphic lymphoid cells and is identified by markers like CD20, CD3, or CD45. The presence of alveolar patterns, cross-striations, and muscle markers (desmin, myogenin) points to rhabdomyosarcoma, not lymphoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: trong>All local anesthetic acts by inhibiting Na+ channels. Mechanism of action & absorption: Site: acts on nodes of ranvier Blocks transmission of pain impulse from nociceptor to spinal cord. Acts on intracellular side of Na channels at inactivation gate blocking the channel. LA doesn’t affect RMP of nerves. Blocks inactivation gates of Na+ channels → Disrupts depolarisation → No action potential generated → No pain sensation. Highest systemic absorption (routes of administration): IV route >Tracheal > Intercostal > Brachial plexus > Epidural. Form for onset of LA action (to reach target nerve) - Unionized form. Active form at site of block of Na channels- Ionized form. Higher doses will act for longer duration and lower doses for a relatively shorter duration. Duration of onset for different local anesthetics (infiltration anesthesia): Short Duration Procaine Chloroprocaine Moderate Duration Lidocaine Prilocaine Long Duration Bupivacaine Ropivacaine Shortest acting - Chloroprocaine Longest acting - Dibucaine Fastest onset - Chloroprocaine (low potency so high concentration used) > Lignocaine (pka is near physiological pH) @Neet_pg_bot

trong>All local anesthetic acts by inhibiting Na+ channels.

Mechanism of action & absorption:

  • Site: acts on nodes of ranvier
  • Blocks transmission of pain impulse from nociceptor to spinal cord.
  • Acts on intracellular side of Na channels at inactivation gate blocking the channel.
  • LA doesn’t affect RMP of nerves.
  • Blocks inactivation gates of Na+ channels → Disrupts depolarisation → No action potential generated → No pain sensation.
  • Highest systemic absorption (routes of administration): IV route >Tracheal > Intercostal > Brachial plexus > Epidural.
  • Form for onset of LA action (to reach target nerve) - Unionized form.
  • Active form at site of block of Na channels- Ionized form.
  • Higher doses will act for longer duration and lower doses for a relatively shorter duration.

 

Duration of onset for different local anesthetics (infiltration anesthesia):

Short Duration
  • Procaine
  • Chloroprocaine

Moderate Duration
  • Lidocaine
  • Prilocaine

Long Duration
  • Bupivacaine
  • Ropivacaine
  • Shortest acting- Chloroprocaine
  • Longest acting- Dibucaine
  • Fastest onset- Chloroprocaine (low potency so high concentration used) > Lignocaine (pka is near physiological pH)

questions.solution: ion is consistent with homocystinuria , which is caused by a deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) . Classical Homocystinuria: Pathogenesis Defective metabolism of methionine and homocysteine Accumulation of homocysteine and methionine Decreased cysteine levels Impaired folate metabolism (in MTHFR deficiency) Enzymes Involved Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) - Most common Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) Defect in methylcobalamin metabolism Clinical Features Ectopia lentis (Inferonasal subluxation of lens) (Superotemporal seen in Marfan disease) Marfanoid habitus (tall, slender, elongated limbs) Developmental delay and intellectual disability Psychiatric and behavioral disorders Skeletal abnormalities (scoliosis, pectus excavatum) Thromboembolism (recurrent episodes of stroke) (due to oxidised homocysteine) Fair complexion, blue eyes Seizures (in ~20% of untreated patients) Diagnosis Elevated homocysteine and methionine in blood and urine Low or absent cysteine in plasma Management Coenzyme supplementation B9 and B12 supplementation Methionine-restricted diet Cysteine supplementation Phenylalanine hydroxylase: This enzyme is deficient in phenylketonuria (PKU), not homocystinuria (Option A) Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) (Option C): While a deficiency of this enzyme can cause a form of non-classical homocystinuria, it typically presents with low or low-normal methionine levels, unlike the elevated methionine seen in this case. This is because MTHFR deficiency leads to THF deficiency, causing less conversion of homocysteine to methionine. Methionine synthase (Option D): Deficiency of this enzyme can cause homocystinuria, but it's typically associated with low methionine levels and methylmalonic aciduria if B12 deficiency is present. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ion is consistent with homocystinuria, which is caused by a deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS).
  •  

    • Classical Homocystinuria:

    Pathogenesis
    • Defective metabolism of methionine and homocysteine
    • Accumulation of homocysteine and methionine
    • Decreased cysteine levels
    • Impaired folate metabolism (in MTHFR deficiency)

    Enzymes Involved
    • Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) - Most common
    • Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR)
    • Defect in methylcobalamin metabolism

    Clinical Features
    • Ectopia lentis (Inferonasal subluxation of lens) (Superotemporal seen in Marfan disease)
    • Marfanoid habitus (tall, slender, elongated limbs)
    • Developmental delay and intellectual disability
    • Psychiatric and behavioral disorders
    • Skeletal abnormalities (scoliosis, pectus excavatum)
    • Thromboembolism (recurrent episodes of stroke) (due to oxidised homocysteine)
    • Fair complexion, blue eyes
    • Seizures (in ~20% of untreated patients)

    Diagnosis
    • Elevated homocysteine and methionine in blood and urine
    • Low or absent cysteine in plasma

    Management
    • Coenzyme supplementation
    • B9 and B12 supplementation
    • Methionine-restricted diet
    • Cysteine supplementation

     

    Phenylalanine hydroxylase: This enzyme is deficient in phenylketonuria (PKU), not homocystinuria (Option A)

    Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) (Option C): While a deficiency of this enzyme can cause a form of non-classical homocystinuria, it typically presents with low or low-normal methionine levels, unlike the elevated methionine seen in this case. This is because MTHFR deficiency leads to THF deficiency, causing less conversion of homocysteine to methionine.

    Methionine synthase (Option D): Deficiency of this enzyme can cause homocystinuria, but it's typically associated with low methionine levels and methylmalonic aciduria if B12 deficiency is present.

questions.solution: uo;s presentation, along with the linear distribution of nodules, is suggestive of sporotrichosis/ Rose Gardner’s disease caused by Sporothrix schenckii. It is a Subcutaneous fungal infection that typically occurs after the fungus is traumatically inoculated into the skin, often through thorn pricks, splinters, or scratches from contaminated plant materials. Enzymes secreted by fungus, such as serine & aspartate proteinases help in local invasion. Sporothrix schenckii has a tendency to spread along lymphatics . questions.stemHtml: A 32 year old male involved in smuggling accidentally swallowed a foreign object, which became lodged in his piriform fossa. After its removal, he reports numbness and loss of sensation in his throat. Which nerve is most likely damaged during the procedure?
questions.solution: is responsible for sensory innervation to the supraglottic region of the larynx, and damage during foreign body removal from the piriform fossa can cause anesthesia in this area. The piriform fossa is a small depression found on each side of the laryngopharynx. It is positioned on both sides of the laryngeal inlet. The boundaries of the piriform fossa include: Medial boundary: Aryepiglottic fold Lateral boundary: Thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane The internal laryngeal nerve runs just beneath the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Damage to the internal laryngeal nerve, such as during the removal of foreign bodies from the fossa, can result in loss of sensation (anesthesia) in the supraglottic region of the larynx. Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A): This nerve innervates the muscles of the larynx and is not the specific nerve affected during this procedure. External laryngeal nerve (Option B): This nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle but does not affect sensory innervation to the supraglottic part of the larynx. Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D): While it provides sensory innervation to the pharynx, it does not innervate the supraglottic part of the larynx. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: has WPW syndrome, indicated by the ECG findings of a short PR interval and a delta wave, along with his symptoms of palpitations and dizziness. Procainamide is the most appropriate drug for treating WPW syndrome with atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). It effectively slows conduction through both the accessory pathway and the atrioventricular (AV) node, aiding in the restoration of normal sinus rhythm. For WPW syndrome: Used with propafenone for narrow QRS tachycardia Used with propafenone, verapamil, or propranolol for wide QRS tachycardia Lidocaine (Option A): Lidocaine is primarily used for ventricular arrhythmias and is not effective for atrial arrhythmias associated with WPW syndrome. Esmolol (Option B): Not recommended in WPW syndrome as it may enhance conduction through the accessory pathway, potentially worsening the arrhythmia. Ajmaline (Option D): Ajmaline, a new Class 1a drug, is not used for treating arrhythmias but is employed in diagnosing Brugada syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: In a 65 y/o male with COPD showing signs of a bacterial respiratory infection, the sputum sample undergoes culture and sensitivity testing using the Epsilometer (E-test). Following incubation, an elliptical zone of inhibition is observed around the antibiotic strip. What is the primary advantage of using the E-test in this clinical context?

options.label: A
options.text: It identifies the specific bacterium causing the infection.

options.label: B
options.text: It determines the bacterium's resistance to all known antibiotics.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides a visual and precise measurement of the minimum inhibitory concentration of the antibiotic.

options.label: D

questions.answerText: It provides a visual and precise measurement of the minimum inhibitory concentration of the antibiotic.
questions.solution: s="customMeta" data-dictid="ff6b4f4d491692777181a02bad075e">antibiotic that inhibits the growth of the bacterium. This helps clinicians choose the most effective antibiotic and dosage for treatment. {{caption_text}} Image showing E-test Step Description Setup An absorbent strip with a gradient of antibiotic concentrations is placed on a culture plate inoculated with the bacterium. Process The strip releases the antibiotic, creating a gradient in the medium. An elliptical zone of inhibition forms around the strip after incubation. Determination The MIC is identified at the point where the edge of the ellipse intersects with the strip, representing the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that inhibits bacterial growth (MIC). It identifies the specific bacterium causing the infection (Option A): The E-test assesses bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics but does not identify the specific bacterium. Step

Description

Setup

An absorbent strip with a gradient of antibiotic concentrations is placed on a culture plate inoculated with the bacterium.

Process

The strip releases the antibiotic, creating a gradient in the medium. An elliptical zone of inhibition forms around the strip after incubation.

Determination

It determines the bacterium's resistance to all known antibiotics (Option B): The E-test measures the MIC for specific antibiotics tested, not for all known antibiotics. Multiple E-tests with different antibiotics can be performed to get a broader resistance profile, but each test is specific to one antibiotic.

It allows for the immediate administration of antibiotics without further testing (Option D): While the E-test provides valuable information, it still requires incubation and interpretation time. questions.solution: a-dictid="ddb3fc5499169277719282f6100904">meniscal tear is locking of the knee during movement. This symptom, along with the “catching” sensation and joint line tenderness, strongly suggests a meniscal injury Meniscal Injuries: Anatomy of the Menisci Location: Fibrocartilaginous structures between femur and tibia in the knee joint. Types: Medial Meniscus: Inner side of the knee; less mobile and more prone to injury due to capsule attachments. Lateral Meniscus: Outer side of the knee; more mobile than the medial meniscus. Structure: Composed of circumferential collagen fibers with radial strands; prone to longitudinal tears. Functions: Aids proprioception through mechanoreceptors that detect joint motion and position. Enhance joint stability and congruency. Facilitate smooth knee motion. Distribute load during weight-bearing (50% in extension; up to 90% in flexion). Mechanism of Meniscal Tears Common Causes: Rotational and Shearing Forces: Twisting a flexed knee under weight (common in sports). Age-Related Degeneration: Reduced mobility in older adults leads to tears with minimal force. Tear Mechanism by Age: Younger Individuals: Traumatic tears from specific sports incidents. Older Individuals: Tears may occur with less force due to degenerative changes, often without a distinct injury. Clinical Features of Meniscal Tears Symptom/ Feature Description Pain Localized to the joint line, particularly medial; worsens with activities stressing the meniscus. Swelling Delayed onset, usually hours after injury; presents as effusion. (Option A ruled out) Mechanical Symptoms Locking: Difficulty fully extending the knee; suggests "bucket-handle" tear. (Option C) Catching: Sensation of knee getting stuck, indicating loose fragment. Giving Way: Knee buckling during twisting movements, suggesting instability. Examination Findings Tenderness: Localized along the joint line, typically medial. Limited Extension: Difficulty achieving full knee extension. Quadriceps Wasting: Possible in chronic cases. Special Tests: Clinical tests ( McMurray's, Apley's, Thessaly) assist diagnosis; MRI is the gold standard. Pain on passive extension (Option B) is more indicative of ligamentous injuries rather than meniscal tears. Dislocation of the knee (Option D) joint is not a feature of meniscal tears; it suggests a more severe injury or instability. @Neet_pg_bot

    •  

    Meniscal Injuries:

    Anatomy of the Menisci

    • Location: Fibrocartilaginous structures between femur and tibia in the knee joint.
    • Types:
      • Medial Meniscus: Inner side of the knee; less mobile and more prone to injury due to capsule attachments.
      • Lateral Meniscus: Outer side of the knee; more mobile than the medial meniscus.
    • Structure: Composed of circumferential collagen fibers with radial strands; prone to longitudinal tears.
    • Functions:
      • Aids proprioception through mechanoreceptors that detect joint motion and position.
      • Enhance joint stability and congruency.
      • Facilitate smooth knee motion.
      • Distribute load during weight-bearing (50% in extension; up to 90% in flexion).

    Mechanism of Meniscal Tears

    • Common Causes:
      • Rotational and Shearing Forces: Twisting a flexed knee under weight (common in sports).
      • Age-Related Degeneration: Reduced mobility in older adults leads to tears with minimal force.
    • Tear Mechanism by Age:
      • Younger Individuals: Traumatic tears from specific sports incidents.
      • Older Individuals: Tears may occur with less force due to degenerative changes, often without a distinct injury.


     

    Clinical Features of Meniscal Tears

    Symptom/ Feature

    Description

    Pain

    Localized to the joint line, particularly medial; worsens with activities stressing the meniscus.

    Swelling

    Delayed onset, usually hours after injury; presents as effusion. (Option A ruled out)

    Mechanical Symptoms
    • Locking: Difficulty fully extending the knee; suggests "bucket-handle" tear. (Option C)
    • Catching: Sensation of knee getting stuck, indicating loose fragment.
    • Giving Way: Knee buckling during twisting movements, suggesting instability.

    Examination Findings
    • Tenderness: Localized along the joint line, typically medial.
    • Limited Extension: Difficulty achieving full knee extension.
    • Quadriceps Wasting: Possible in chronic cases.
    • Special Tests: Clinical tests (McMurray's, Apley's, Thessaly) assist diagnosis; MRI is the gold standard.

     

    Pain on passive extension (Option B) is more indicative of ligamentous injuries rather than meniscal tears.

     

    Dislocation of the knee (Option D) joint is not a feature of meniscal tears; it suggests a more severe injury or instability.

Dementia with Lewy Bodies

  • Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline sufficient to interfere with social or occupational functioning.
  • Early symptoms may include difficulties with attention, fronto-subcortical skills, and visuospatial ability, rather than prominent memory issues.

 

Clinical Features:

Probable DLB requires two or more core symptoms, while possible DLB requires at least one.

Core Features

Supporting Features
  • Fluctuating levels of attention and alertness (Option A ruled out)
  • Recurrent visual hallucinations (Option B ruled out)
  • Parkinsonian features (e.g., cogwheeling, bradykinesia, resting tremor) (Option D ruled out)
  • REM Sleep behavior disorder
  • Repeated falls
  • Syncope
  • Sensitivity to neuroleptics
  • Systematized delusions (Option C)
  • Hallucinations in other modalities (e.g., auditory, tactile)

 

Differences in features of LBD and PD:

Feature

Lewy Body Dementia (LBD)

Parkinson's Disease (PD)

Onset of Symptoms

Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms appear early; motor symptoms develop later.

Primarily motor symptoms appear first (e.g., bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors).

Visual Hallucinations

Common and can occur early.

Less common initially; may occur later, often due to treatment.

Fluctuations in Attention

Fluctuations in alertness and attention are characteristic.

Fluctuations are primarily related to medication cycles.

Response to Medications

Poor response to dopaminergic medications; risk of worsening psychiatric symptoms.

Generally improves with dopaminergic medications (e.g., levodopa).

Sleep Disturbances

REM sleep behavior disorder is common and can precede cognitive symptoms.

REM sleep behavior disorder may occur but is primarily linked to motor symptoms.

Progression

Rapid progression of cognitive and behavioral symptoms.

Gradual progression of motor symptoms, with cognitive decline developing later.

 

Pathology:

  • Lewy body disease presents clinically similarly to Alzheimer’s disease but is marked by hallucinations, parkinsonian features, and extrapyramidal signs.
  • Lewy bodies, which are abnormal accumulations of α-synuclein aggregates, are found in the cerebral cortex and substantia nigra.
  • In cases where Lewy body pathology coexists with Alzheimer’s, the amygdala is often the only affected region.
  • Patients with Lewy body dementia may exhibit Capgras syndrome (reduplicative paramnesia), highlighting the complex nature of their symptoms.

In a lateral chest X-ray, the hilar region is typically located posteriorly and laterally within the mediastinum.

Focusing on area B allows for optimal visualization of structures such as the pulmonary arteries, veins, and lymph nodes, which are critical in identifying potential pathologies like tumors, infections, or vascular changes.

Area B is best suited for assessing any abnormalities that may indicate underlying disease in the hilar region.

Fissures of the Lung and Hemidiaphragm in Chest Radiography

 

Lung Fissures in Chest Radiography

 

Right Lung

Left Lung

Three lobes: Upper, Middle, Lower

Two lobes: Upper, Lower

Fissures:

Horizontal fissure: Separates the upper and middle lobes.

Oblique fissure: Separates the middle from the lower lobe, and also divides the upper from the lower lobe.

Fissures:

Oblique (major) fissure: Separates the upper from the lower lobe.


Clinical Relevance:

  • Right Middle Lobe (RML) Collapse: Seen as a wedge-shaped opacity overlying the heart on lateral X-ray.
  • Lobar Pneumonia: Fissures localize consolidation (e.g., obscured right heart border in RML pneumonia).
  • Pleural Effusion: Blunts fissures due to fluid accumulation.


 

Elevated Hemidiaphragm

Flat Hemidiaphragm

One side of the diaphragm appears higher than normal.

The normally dome-shaped diaphragm appears flattened and lower in position.

Causes:

 
  • Subphrenic Abscess: Pus beneath diaphragm.
  • Hepatomegaly/Splenomegaly: Enlarged organs push the diaphragm upward.
  • Diaphragmatic Palsy: Paralysis due to phrenic nerve injury.
  • Lung Collapse/Fibrosis: Loss of lung volume elevates the diaphragm.
  • Atelectasis: Collapsed lung leads to diaphragm elevation.

Causes:

 
  • COPD: Hyperinflated lungs cause a flat diaphragm and tubular heart appearance.
  • Tension Pneumothorax: Air pushes the diaphragm downward.
  • Emphysema: Destruction of lung tissue results in diaphragm flattening.
