questions.stem: A 36 y/o woman, G3P2, delivered via C-section 4 hours ago and is now experiencing severe PPH unresponsive to uterine massage and uterotonics. Her vital signs show tachycardia and hypotension. The medical team opts for surgical intervention to avoid a hysterectomy. What is the principle behind performing bilateral internal iliac artery ligation to control her PPH?
questions.stemHtml: A 36 y/o woman, G3P2, delivered via C-section 4 hours ago and is now experiencing severe PPH unresponsive to uterine massage and uterotonics. Her vital signs show tachycardia and hypotension. The medical team opts for surgical intervention to avoid a hysterectomy. What is the principle behind performing bilateral internal iliac artery ligation to control her PPH?

options.label: A
options.text: To apply direct pressure on the bleeding site

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce distal blood flow and convert arterial pressure to venous-like pressure

options.label: C
options.text: To increase uterine contractility and reduce bleeding

options.label: D
options.text: To promote rapid healing of uterine tissues

questions.answerText: To reduce distal blood flow and convert arterial pressure to venous-like pressure
questions.solution: he principle of bilateral internal iliac artery ligation is to reduce blood flow to the uterus and pelvis , significantly lowering pulse pressure (85% reduction) in arteries distal to the ligation. This reduction in pressure makes the blood vessels more conducive to hemostasis through clot formation, similar to venous circulation. Considerations: Ligation of the internal iliac artery is to be done at 5cm distal to common iliac bifurcation - this avoids the posterior division branches of the internal iliac artery. Should not perforate continuous large veins, esp. Internal iliac vein. Non-absorbable sutures are used. To apply direct pressure on the bleeding site (Option A) is not the goal of internal iliac artery ligation; this applies to uterine tamponade or manual compression. To increase uterine contractility and reduce bleeding (Option C) is achieved with uterotonics, not artery ligation. To promote rapid healing of uterine tissues (Option D): Internal iliac artery ligation controls bleeding by reducing blood flow, not by promoting tissue healing. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
he principle of bilateral internal iliac artery ligation is to reduce blood flow to the uterus and pelvis, significantly lowering pulse pressure (85% reduction) in arteries distal to the ligation.
  • This reduction in pressure makes the blood vessels more conducive to hemostasis through clot formation, similar to venous circulation.
  • Considerations:
    • Ligation of the internal iliac artery is to be done at 5cm distal to common iliac bifurcation - this avoids the posterior division branches of the internal iliac artery.
    • Should not perforate continuous large veins, esp. Internal iliac vein.
    • Non-absorbable sutures are used.

    • To apply direct pressure on the bleeding site (Option A) is not the goal of internal iliac artery ligation; this applies to uterine tamponade or manual compression.

     

    To increase uterine contractility and reduce bleeding (Option C) is achieved with uterotonics, not artery ligation.

     

    To promote rapid healing of uterine tissues (Option D): Internal iliac artery ligation controls bleeding by reducing blood flow, not by promoting tissue healing.

questions.stem: A 55 y/o male heart transplant patient comes for a follow-up visit. He reports that he has been engaging in moderate exercise for about 30 minutes daily. Despite lacking sympathetic innervation to his transplanted heart, he notices an increase in his stamina and ability to exercise over time. Given the patient's condition, what physiological mechanism allows him to experience an increase in cardiac output during exercise?
questions.stemHtml:
A 55 y/o male heart transplant patient comes for a follow-up visit. He reports that he has been engaging in moderate exercise for about 30 minutes daily. Despite lacking sympathetic innervation to his transplanted heart, he notices an increase in his stamina and ability to exercise over time.
Given the patient's condition, what physiological mechanism allows him to experience an increase in cardiac output during exercise?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased heart rate through parasympathetic withdrawal.

options.label: B
options.text: An enhanced force of contraction via the Frank-Starling mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Parasympathetic stimulation reduces heart rate variability.

options.label: D
options.text: Increased heart rate through sympathetic stimulation to heart.

questions.answerText: An enhanced force of contraction via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
questions.solution: dictid="b7eed7d7e816927771995e0a067401">stroke volume by enhancing the force of contraction in response to increased venous return during exercise, thereby increasing cardiac output. While parasympathetic withdrawal can lead to a slight increase in heart rate, it is not the primary mechanism by which cardiac output is increased in a heart transplant patient during exercise (Option A). Aspect Details Frank-Starling Mechanism More heart muscle stretch during filling leads to stronger contractions and higher stroke volume. Sympathetic Innervation Lost in heart transplant patients; cannot increase heart rate through the sympathetic nervous system. (Option D) Parasympathetic Innervation Lost in heart transplant patients; cannot decrease heart rate through the parasympathetic nervous system. (Option C) Stroke Volume Increase Achieved by increased force of contraction in response to increased venous return during exercise. Cardiac Output Increased primarily due to higher stroke volume, not heart rate. Comparison to Healthy Individuals Less increase in cardiac output, relying on stroke volume rather than both stroke volume and heart rate. So, in transplant patients,the increase in cardiac output during exercise is mainly due to an increase in stroke volume, not heart rate. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
dictid="b7eed7d7e816927771995e0a067401">stroke volume by enhancing the force of contraction in response to increased venous return during exercise, thereby increasing cardiac output.

While parasympathetic withdrawal can lead to a slight increase in heart rate, it is not the primary mechanism by which cardiac output is increased in a heart transplant patient during exercise(Option A).

 

Aspect

Details

Frank-Starling Mechanism

More heart muscle stretch during filling leads to stronger contractions and higher stroke volume.

Sympathetic Innervation

Lost in heart transplant patients; cannot increase heart rate through the sympathetic nervous system. (Option D)

Parasympathetic Innervation

Lost in heart transplant patients; cannot decrease heart rate through the parasympathetic nervous system. (Option C)

Stroke Volume Increase

Achieved by increased force of contraction in response to increased venous return during exercise.

Cardiac Output

Increased primarily due to higher stroke volume, not heart rate.

Comparison to Healthy Individuals

Less increase in cardiac output, relying on stroke volume rather than both stroke volume and heart rate.

So, in transplant patients,the increase in cardiac output during exercise is mainly due to an increase in stroke volume, not heart rate.

Mendelson’s Syndrome - serious and life-threatening complication caused by aspiration of gastric contents (pH <2.5) under general anesthesia in young and healthy obstetrical patients (especially during cesarean section). Predisposing Factors Delayed gastric emptying (Option D) due to: High serum progesterone levels (Option A) , decreased motilin (Option B, or m aternal apprehension during labor (Option C) Complications Chemical pneumonitis Lung damage Atelectasis Bronchopneumonia Clinical features Commonly Affected lobe: Right lower lobe (due to aspiration through the right bronchus). Tachycardia Tachypnea Bronchospasm Rhonchi Rales Cyanosis Decreased PaO₂ Hypotension Diagnosis Chest X-ray reveals right lower lobe involvement. Management Immediate suctioning of the oropharynx and nasopharynx to remove inhaled fluid. Bronchoscopy if large particulate matter is present. questions.solutionHtml:
lanation:

The clinical scenario is consistent with the diagnosis of Mendelson’s syndrome. Increased gastric motility is not a predisposing factor for Mendelson’s syndrome.

 

Mendelson’s Syndrome- serious and life-threatening complication caused by aspiration of gastric contents (pH <2.5) under general anesthesia in young and healthy obstetrical patients (especially during cesarean section).
Predisposing Factors

Delayed gastric emptying (Option D) due to: High serum progesterone levels (Option A), decreased motilin (Option B, or maternal apprehension during labor (Option C)
Complications
  • Chemical pneumonitis
  • Lung damage
  • Atelectasis
  • Bronchopneumonia

Clinical features

Commonly Affected lobe: Right lower lobe (due to aspiration through the right bronchus).

  • Tachycardia
  • Tachypnea
  • Bronchospasm
  • Rhonchi
  • Rales
  • Cyanosis
  • Decreased PaO₂
  • Hypotension
Diagnosis Chest X-ray reveals right lower lobe involvement.
Management
  • Immediate suctioning of the oropharynx and nasopharynx to remove inhaled fluid.
  • Bronchoscopy if large particulate matter is present.
  • Continuous positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) to maintain arterial oxygen saturation at 95%.
  • Administration of antibiotics if infection is evident.
